articles.title: Carney, Smith say new West Coast pipeline could get oil companies building again
articles.summary: It's been a relatively quiet decade in Alberta's oilsands, but the federal and provincial governments believe a new West Coast pipeline coupled with policy shifts might help turn up the volume. Prime…

image.caption: Oilsands companies have for years shied away from building multibillion-dollar megaprojects like the Suncor Fort Hills facility in Fort McMurray, Alta., which opened in 2018. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

It's been a relatively quiet decade in Alberta's oilsands, but the federal and provincial governments believe a new West Coast pipeline coupled with policy shifts might help turn up the volume. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith say that if oilsands companies start building again — as they hope — it will be different this time around.
This time, sector is ready to heat up without the headaches, leaders say
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 02, 2026 5:02 PM EDT | Last Updated: 11 minutes ago
It's been a relatively quiet decade in Alberta's oilsands, but the federal and provincial governments believe a new West Coast pipeline coupled with policy shifts might help turn up the volume.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Fort McMurray, Alta., this week to announce the first proposal to be deemed in the national interest under legislation passed last year: the million-barrel-per-day Pacific Link pipeline from Alberta to a tanker export terminal in southern B.C.
The designation means the proposal will be subject to a streamlined review process, shepherded by the Calgary-based major projects office.

The pipeline's economic fate hinges on oilsands companies being willing to spend on expanding their output. At a news conference, Carney was asked whether he expected a return to boom times in the northeastern Alberta oilsands hub city.
"I wouldn't use the term 'boom,"' he replied. "I would use 'sustained growth."'
Carney designates West Coast pipeline a project of national interest

The last boom from the mid-2000s to mid-2010s came with the side-effects of cost inflation, labour scarcity and housing shortages. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith say that if oilsands companies start building again — as they hope — it will be different this time around.
Oilsands companies have for years shied away from the multibillion-dollar megaprojects of more than a decade ago. The last mine to be built from scratch was Fort Hills, operated by Suncor Energy Inc.
From when it got the final go-ahead decision in 2013 to its startup in 2018, its cost ballooned to more than $17 billion from $13.5 billion.
Lately, instead of so-called "green field" projects, companies have opted to instead tweak their existing operations to squeeze out more bitumen or add to their existing footprints.
Executives have cited a dearth of pipeline capacity, a convoluted regulatory regime and onerous environmental regulations for the chill on large-scale growth projects.

[Companies] have managed to find a way to increase production without having the kind of dramatic pressure that we saw in the past of a large number of people moving here, not able to find homes.- Danielle Smith, Alberta premier

But also around the time investment fell off a decade ago, global crude prices cratered amid a supply glut and didn't have much of a chance to recover before the COVID-19 pandemic virtually obliterated demand.
Fast forward to 2026, and the Mideast war has laid bare the vulnerability of global energy supply chains and left countries clamouring for stable providers.

A host of Trudeau-era energy policies loathed by oilpatch players have been undone and Pacific Link has taken a big step forward to becoming a reality, potentially enabling more oilsands crude to reach lucrative Asian markets.
"We learned lessons from the past in building infrastructure," Carney told reporters on Thursday.
He said local mayors are thinking ahead for what their communities need and early participation from First Nations leaders means "a much broader spread of the economic benefits."
He also cited "another phase of technical innovation" in the industry that didn't exist previously.
More mature oil sector
At the news conference, Smith noted the autonomous oilsands haul trucks in the backdrop.

Previously, human drivers for those gargantuan vehicles would have received six-figure salaries and might have been flown in and out of the site from elsewhere in Canada, living in work camps, for a week or two at a time.

"[Companies] have managed to find a way to increase production without having the kind of dramatic pressure that we saw in the past of a large number of people moving here, not able to find homes," Smith said.
The premier said she's also talked to local municipal leaders about the bridge and road infrastructure that might be needed if production ramps up.
She mentioned upgrades to Highway 881, the road that winds through several steam-driven oilsands sites south of Fort McMurray.
"There's lots of ways that we can partner with the federal government to make sure those key infrastructure projects get built, so we build on a pace that allows us to keep up," she said.
Andrew Botterill, who leads Deloitte Canada's oil, gas and chemicals practice, said the Alberta oilpatch has matured since the last boom.
"What we have is a more efficient, far more aligned group of producers up there than maybe what it was 10, 15 years ago," he said.

"They've come together as an alliance and really recognize that 'We've got to share labour, we've got to be less competitive, we've got to find ways that we can do things together and not just drive up costs."'
LISTEN | One million barrels a day:
The Current7:28Canada’s new Pacific Link Pipeline

Oilsands properties are concentrated in fewer hands than had been the case a decade or more ago. Erstwhile producers including Husky and MEG Energy have been bought out and international players like Shell and Total have exited or sharply reduced their holdings.

Lance Mortlock, managing partner at EY Canada, flagged a bigger-picture concern: With multiple major projects in the works — not just the Pacific Link pipeline and new oilsands projects, but potentially mines, transmission lines and hydro dams — will there be enough workers?

"We're going to need tens of thousands of workers across the country to build this stuff: engineers, professionals, welders, pipefitters. I'm not sure where all these people are going to come from if we do half the projects that we have the desire to construct," he said.
"So I'm hoping that there's going to be more conversation about the workforce and more conversation about how do we sequence these things so we optimize the system from a labour force perspective."

articles.title: Disgraced gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar removed from Michigan sex offender registry
articles.summary: Convicted offender among 20,000 people removed from list after state supreme court ruling on Sora registration law

blocks.text: Larry Nassar, the former Michigan State University and USA Gymnastics physician convicted of sexually abusing girls and women over a period of decades while claiming to provide medical treatment, has been removed from Michigan’s sex offender registry thanks to a legal technicality.
Thousands of other offenders were also taken off that list after a court ruling involving how the state’s registration law can be applied.

On 9 September, the Michigan supreme court ruled that the state’s sex offender registration act (Sora) cannot be applied retroactively to cases involving offenses committed before the law’s relevant date. Michigan’s state police, as a result, removed more than 20,000 people whose offenses occurred before 1 July 2011 from the agency’s online sex offender database.

Nassar, 63, was among those removed. The Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office – which was among the agencies to prosecute him – confirmed Nassar’s absence from the registry by sharing a screenshot showing a search for his name returning zero results.

“The Michigan supreme court’s decision to eliminate Sora requirements for these offenders is deeply concerning,” the attorney’s office said in a statement. “Our community, along with the victims of these crimes, expected the registry to provide a measure of protection and awareness – assurances that have now been removed by the court’s ruling.”

In another post, the prosecutor’s office said that although officials “disagree with the court and have concern about the potential risk created by the decision”, the office is “bound to respect and follow the ruling”.

Michigan lawmakers do not have the authority to reverse the state supreme court’s decision. However, the legislature could pass new legislation that would place the affected offenders back in the database.

Nassar was sentenced in 2018 to as many as 175 years in state and federal prison after being convicted of sexually abusing women and girls for decades while working at Michigan State University and serving as a doctor for Team USA Gymnastics.
As of Friday, Nassar’s projected earliest release date for his federal prison sentence was in 2068, when he would be 104.
More than 150 women and girls have accused Nassar of assault. His accusers include Olympic gold medal-winning gymnasts Aly Raisman, Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney and Gabby Douglas.
Nassar pleaded guilty in November 2017 to multiple counts of first-degree criminal sexual conduct. He survived being stabbed multiple times in July 2023 while imprisoned.
During his sentencing hearing, his accusers delivered impact statements describing the shame and trauma they said they experienced because of Nassar.

articles.title: Ottawa launches new national AI council to advise on safety, deployment
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's new national council on artificial intelligence is meant to provide the government with guidance on the evolution of its AI strategy and on making the technology safer.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen touring the Vector artificial intelligence research institute in Toronto last year. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney's new national council on artificial intelligence is meant to provide the government with guidance on the evolution of its AI strategy and on making the technology safer.
Council members will offer guidance for national AI strategy
Prime Minister Mark Carney has a new national council on artificial intelligence meant to provide the government with guidance for its AI strategy and on making the technology safer.

A news release from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) on Friday outlined the formation of the Prime Minister's National Council on Artificial Intelligence, which looks to convene public and private stakeholders to advise on the evolution of Canada's AI strategy.

The release said the members of the council will advise on accelerating adoption, developing national champions in the industry and building AI infrastructure as well as making AI safer, protecting Canadian democracy and ensuring Canadians benefit from the technology.

"The new National Council on Artificial Intelligence will inform and advise the government on how to most effectively deploy AI in Canada — how to manage the risks, seize the opportunities and ensure AI is used to improve the lives of all Canadians," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement.
Over a dozen members were named to the council.

One is Yoshua Bengio, considered one of the godfathers of AI. Bengio's company LawZero is focused on developing a safe by design AI model called Scientist AI and was on the receiving end of $150 million in federal funding last month.

items: Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?

blocks.text: Another AI leader in the group is Valérie Pisano, CEO of Mila — one of Canada's national AI institutes and a non-profit committed to advancing AI for the benefit of all.

The council includes Sen. Tom Pitfield, who was appointed by Carney to the Red Chamber in July. Pitfield was previously one of Carney's top advisers, serving on his election campaign team and later in the PMO.
Patrick Pichette joins the council as CEO of Digital Transformation Canada, a new agency seeking to modernize federal services. Pichette is also a member of Canada's AI strategy task force.
AI's risks in the spotlight
The announcement comes as experts and stakeholders worldwide are pushing for caution around AI's rapid development.

In July, hundreds of rogue OpenAI agents escaped human control and hacked into the online platform Hugging Face, promoting an open letter from more than 100 companies cautioning AI-powered cyberattacks will become more frequent and complex as the technology gets stronger.
Existential warnings about AI 'are not new,' minister says
Last month, an outgoing researcher at leading AI company Anthropic provided a dire warning in a thread on X that AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade, garnering widespread attention.
Days later, Anthropic's CEO, Dario Amodei, published an essay which called on the AI industry to slow its rapid development so safety measures could catch up to the technology.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Actor and advocate Michael J. Fox promoted to companion level in Order of Canada
articles.summary: Spectators stood and applauded Michael J. Fox at Rideau Hall on Friday as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially named the celebrated actor and Parkinson's disease activist to the companion level of the…

image.caption: Michael J. Fox is seen being invested as a companion of the Order of Canada by Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour at Rideau Hall in Ottawa on Friday. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Spectators stood and applauded Michael J. Fox at Rideau Hall on Friday as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially named the celebrated actor and Parkinson's disease activist to the companion level of the Order of Canada.
'Back to the Future' star among 51 people inducted into, or promoted within, the Order of Canada on Friday

Spectators stood to applaud Michael J. Fox at Rideau Hall on Friday as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially promoted the celebrated actor and Parkinson's disease activist to companion of the Order of Canada.
Rideau Hall said Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his "powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson's."
Parkinson's is a progressive nervous system disorder that causes tremors, stiffness and slowness and is linked to depression and memory problems.

Fox, who went public with his Parkinson's diagnosis in 1998, has raised funds for research into the disease and has shared candid experiences about the challenges faced by those living with its symptoms.
Michael J. Fox promoted within Order of Canada
He was among 51 people inducted into, or promoted within, the Order of Canada on Friday.
Arbour said each inductee had demonstrated excellence and thanked them for their work.
"You could have used your talents solely to further your own success. Instead, you have chosen to use your skills, influence and energy to help others," said in French.
"Because talent, as exceptional as it may be, is not sufficient on its own. It also takes the will to get involved and to take action to improve one's community and contribute to the common good."
Arbour said Fox is a "shining example of this."
"Your example reminds us of something that's very fundamental: sustainable progress requires that we move forward with courage, imagination and determination," she said.
"After all, back to the future has always been a much better idea than forward to the past."
Academics, artists among honourees

Yusuf Altintas, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia, was inducted as an officer of the Order of Canada, along with Nada Jabado, a professor at McGill University who is being honoured for her work in pediatric neuro-oncology.
Former Bank of Canada governor Stephen Poloz was inducted as an officer for helping facilitate Canada's international trade and promote its economic well-being.

Sculptor Ruth Elsie Abernethy was inducted as a member. Rideau Hall said she has created iconic life-size bronze pieces showcased around the world and that her work explores themes of gender, heritage and nation-building.
Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporter Susanne Craig was inducted as a member for her work with The New York Times, The Globe and Mail and The Wall Street Journal.
Rideau Hall described her as one of the most outstanding journalists of her generation, citing her coverage of contemporary issues in the United States.

Colin Roswell Clarke was inducted as a member for his work as founder and artistic director of the Toronto Youth Wind Orchestra program. Marcelle Dubois was inducted a member for her work revitalizing Quebec playwriting.

Patrick Joseph Lahey, co-founder of Triton Submarines, was inducted as a member for his work as one of the world's leading experts on submersibles and a leading voice for safe practices in the deep-diving industry, Rideau Hall said.

articles.summary: The suspect was already charged with the killing of Reform UK's Ann Widdecombe.

image.caption: The suspect allegedly planned acts of terrorism that included an attack on Nigel Farage [File photo: August 13, 2026]Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: A man has been charged with planning acts of terrorism, including against far-right politician and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, British police said.
"We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, saying the investigation resulted in "this very serious charge."
The suspect, Joshua Kerry, was also charged with the murder of former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe.
According to the prosecutor handling the case, Kerry allegedly hit Widdecombe on her head 21 times with a hammer while she had been eating lunch.
Widdecombe's murder triggered reactions from across British politics, including demands to improve lawmakers' security arrangements.
The new charges against Kerry include one count of preparing acts of terrorism for actions allegedly carried out between May 31, 2024 and July 8, 2026.
According to the police's statement, the 28-year-old suspect is due to appear in a London magistrates' court on October 7.

Apart from Widdecombe, two other politicians were murdered this decade. Labor's Jo Cox was murdered by a neo-Nazi sympathizer in 2016 and Conservative David Amees was killed in 2021 by an "Islamic State" supporter.

articles.byline: Adria R Walker in Jackson, Mississippi

blocks.text: Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party.

Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!”

In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state. The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol.

“This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing.

Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others.
Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building.

An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens.
Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record.
“This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.”

The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans, all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision.

And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours.
State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments.

“The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson, who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district.

Through continued boos, White said that there was a “silent majority” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”.
Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal.

“I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.”
Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”.

“The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.”

Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state.

“If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power.

“We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.”

The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.

articles.title: Hawaii’s centuries-old sea arch collapses into Pacific after series of rough storms
articles.summary:
Hōlei sea arch, formed 550 years ago by erosion from ocean waves, no longer standing, National Park Service confirms

A famed centuries-old sea arch on Hawaii’s remote and rugged coastline…

blocks.text: A famed centuries-old sea arch on Hawaii’s remote and rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean, the National Park Service confirmed on Friday, following a stretch of rough storms in the region in recent weeks.

The beloved landmark, Hōlei sea arch, stood at around 90ft high for over half a millennium in Hawaii’s Volcanoes national park, located on the dramatic southern coast of the Big Island. It was naturally formed around 550 years ago due to differential erosion by ocean waves.

The exact timing of the collapse is unknown. The National Park Service (NPS) said the arch was still standing on Wednesday 23 September, when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo, but had collapsed by Sunday night, on 27 September.

“The arch formed in ancient lava flows by removing rock along cracks and weaker rocks,” the US Geological Survey said in a description of the arch in 2014. “It will not be here for ever. Every day the ocean crashes against the pillar of the arch, eroding it a little more. One day, it will be gone.”

Indeed, the cliffs on either side of the sea arch had shown signs of instability for years amid tropical systems and volcanic activity, the NPS said, meaning the arch’s collapse had long been expected.

Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcanic eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs around the arch. Then, in January 2020, new cracks and instability prompted the park to close the original viewing area and open a safer one further from the cliff edge three months later. Later that year, huge surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the arch’s lower portion.

The Hawaiian islands have seen an unusually high number of severe storms this year, with storm activity in the Pacific running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. Experts say the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

Nolo, which rapidly intensified into a hurricane on 24 September – causing Volcanoes national park to shutter - was the third major storm to devastate the islands of Hawaii in recent months. Residents were still recovering from hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September, which had flooded homes and roads, toppled trees and caused power outages, when Nolo then battered the islands with heavy rain and high surf.

Forecasters have warned there is a high probability that this “supercharged” El Niño will reach a historic intensity, with its effects in strengthening the storms compounded by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

articles.title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne
articles.summary:
The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am

  • Get our

blocks.text: A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.

Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.
Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.
Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”
Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.
The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.

Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.
The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake.

articles.title: Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community
articles.summary:
The men were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar

Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community.
Rahman Salehi, 35, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police (CTP), said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”

She added: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran. While this incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “We have decided to prosecute Rahman Salehi and Salam Ahmadyan following a fast-paced counter-terrorism policing investigation in Greater Manchester in September targeting the Jewish community.

“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.

“We understand that this case may cause concern, particularly considering the arrests came on the eve of Yom Kippur. We want to assure the Jewish community that working with the police, their safety and that of the wider public is our highest priority.”
The men, both in their 30s, were arrested on 20 September, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
They were arrested in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of the city centre, before being held in custody at a London police station.
Counter-terrorism police had been given more time to question the men, who were detained under section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said: “These recent events are a stark reminder of the threats posed against this country from both terrorists and foreign state actors.

“This news will be deeply distressing for our Jewish communities, coming so soon after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. I know this will be especially true in Manchester, as we mark one year since the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue.

“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country. While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.”
Salehi and Ahmadyan They are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.
The Metropolitan police, who are leading the investigation, said searches had also been carried out at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.

At the time of the arrests, Evans said police officers were “doing everything we can to keep them [the Jewish community] and the wider public safe”, while counter-terrorism police and local forces were working together “to provide protective security support and advice for areas with Jewish communities, and particularly during the High Holy Day period”.
Last year, Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by armed police after launching a terror attack during Yom Kippur at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester.
Two men were killed during the attack, Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, while three others were injured.

articles.title: Stellantis says tariffs, consumer demand driving weeks-long layoffs at Windsor plant
articles.summary: Global carmaker Stellantis says tariffs and consumer demand in North America are driving weeks-long layoffs at the company's plant in Windsor, Ont.

image.caption: A file photo shows workers leaving the Stellantis Windsor Assembly Plant in Windsor, Ont., on April 4, 2025, ahead of a two-week shutdown linked to U.S auto tariffs. The Windsor Assembly Plant will be down once again in late October, the company said Friday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Global carmaker Stellantis says tariffs and consumer demand in North America are driving weeks-long layoffs at the company's plant in Windsor, Ont.
Company, union still at standstill in contract talks

In a statement Friday, Stellantis Canada announced it will idle the plant for three weeks starting later this month. The more than 6,400 employees at the facility were already laid off for the last two weeks and are set to return to work Monday.
"Stellantis continues to evaluate and adjust its manufacturing operations in response to evolving market conditions, including consumer demand and the impact of tariffs," a spokesperson wrote.
"Consistent with those efforts, the Windsor Assembly Plant will be down the weeks of Oct. 19 and 26 as well as Nov. 2."

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
Will auto tariffs be a permanent roadblock for a Canada-U.S. trade deal?

blocks.text: The news of fresh layoffs comes at a time of significant uncertainty for Stellantis workers in Windsor, who build the Chrysler Pacifica minivans and Dodge Charger muscle cars, as well as the carmaker's employees elsewhere in the country.
Stellantis and Unifor, the workers' union, sit at a standstill in contract talks, in large part due to an impasse over the future of the company's assembly plant in Brampton, Ont.
The company has said it wants to sell the plant, citing "market and trade conditions." Unifor has dubbed the plan "indefensible."

items: 'Don't close, don't sell': Union implores Stellantis to keep Brampton plant as automaker signals sale
Ford, Joly call on Stellantis to make new model at Brampton plant after automaker signals potential sale

blocks.text: On Friday, Stellantis said there has been "[n]o change in contract negotiations," and that workers are "following the terms of the expired collective agreement for the time being."
Unifor's collective agreement with Stellantis expired on Sept. 20.
'Something we didn't want to hear': Union leader
James Stewart, president of Unifor Local 444 — which represents the auto workers in Windsor — shared news of the latest layoffs on social media Friday.
"That's more downtime in our system, something we didn't want to hear," Stewart said in a video posted to Facebook.
Stewart has previously said that in addition to the Brampton plant, securing more product allocations for Windsor and the company's casting plant in Etobicoke is an important issue in contract talks.

A representative for Stewart said he was unavailable for an interview Friday. But in the video, Stewart said employees in Windsor will get more information about where negotiations stand upon their return to work Monday.
"We're currently working on a leaflet to update you on some of the things that have been going on in our bargaining, what's happening now and what to expect in the future," he said.
"We know you're looking forward to getting some type of update on the bargaining process."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Emma Loop is a video journalist at CBC Windsor. She previously spent eight years covering politics, national security, and business in Washington, D.C. Before that, she covered Canadian politics in Ottawa. She has worked at the Windsor Star, Ottawa Citizen, Axios, and BuzzFeed News, where she was a member of the FinCEN Files team that was named a finalist for the 2021 Pulitzer Prize in International Reporting. She was born and raised in Essex County, Ont. You can reach her at emma.loop@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage
articles.summary:
Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with…

blocks.text: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage, police have said.

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.

The senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counter Terrorism Policing network.
“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”
Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.

Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.
She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.
Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.

articles.title: Christa Pike remains unconscious and on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee
articles.summary:
Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system

Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe…

blocks.text: Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
The attorneys said hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system as of late Thursday.
Pike received two doses of the drug in a failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute her on Wednesday.
In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with intravenuous lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote.
They also wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” the execution team proceeded to prepare and administer a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 in connection with the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee.
One grim detail about the case is that a satanic symbol had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years.
Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Pike has prompted top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community to call for a moratorium on the death penalty in the US.

articles.title: New York governor condemns handling of Cornell rape case
articles.summary: An 2024 alleged gang rape at the prestigious Cornell University has gained national attention after the accuser, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit. A special prosecutor has been appointed…

image.caption: New York Governor Kathy Hochul (left) appointed Attorney General Letitia James (right) as a special prosecutor to take over the investigationImage: Steve Sanchez/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: New York Governor Kathy Hochul said the accuser of the six Cornell University students of gang rape was "failed" by those whose obligation was protecting her.
This includes both campus police and the county prosecutor, Hochul said.

At a press conference on Friday, she also announced the appointment of Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the investigation due to the fact she had lost faith in the local district attorney's ability to handle the case.
This came after she learned the "troubling" details of the authorities' handling of the accuser's case so far.
"In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked.
"This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."

blocks.caption: Cornell Univesity defended its handling of the caseImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Hochul, the woman, identified only by the placeholder name Jane Doe, told police "exactly what happened to her," including her firm belief that she had been raped.
"Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors."
Investigation to take time
Attorney General Letitia James said she did not know how long her investigation might take.

"I know that you want answers. I do too. A comprehensive investigation of this nature takes time, but my office is committed to seeing it through," James said, adding that evidence gathering and interviews will be carried out.
The original investigation into the case was closed without any charges in 2024.

blocks.caption: Jane Doe's lawsuit in 2026 gained national attentionImage: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who was responsible for the decision, the woman's sworn statement did not include her allegation of being drugged against her will without any ability to consent and forced into sex.
Van Houten reopened the investigation after the accuser filed a new lawsuit in September, 2026, against seven fraternity members, as well as against Cornell.
The lawsuit has since made national headlines and sparked protests at Cornell and across the United States.

blocks.caption: Sanctions have been taken against the Chi Phi fraternity, involved in the caseImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cornell said it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the allegations, while also imposing a range of disciplinary measures.
The school also said it supports James' appointment and is "committed to an independent external review of all aspects" of its handling of the case.

articles.title: King Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tour
articles.summary:
Buckingham Palace say the king will not ‘shy away’ from Britain’s role in slavery when he visits Commonwealth nations later this month

King Charles III will acknowledge the “darkest days” of…

blocks.text: King Charles III will acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery while touring Caribbean countries on a visit beginning this month, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Friday.

The king will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana alone, followed by a trip to Antigua and Barbuda with Queen Camilla, where Charles will give a speech at a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government, the palace said.
Charles, 77, who is still receiving treatment for cancer, will visit former colonies that are now independent from Britain and are members of the British Commonwealth.
He remains head of state in the archipelago nations of the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, a role that is largely ceremonial.
The palace spokesperson told reporters the king’s visit, from 27 October to 4 November, would not “shy away from the ’darkest days of our past’, as His Majesty has described them”.
Charles used the phrase in a speech in Barbados when he attended the ceremony in which it became a republic in 2021, removing his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, as head of state.
He also said then that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” stains Britain’s history.

The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge “the wrongs of the past” and “right inequalities that endure”, and on this trip would “renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process”.
The UK government reiterated last month its rejection of calls for the payment of slavery reparations after a Jamaican delegation filed a petition addressed to Charles on the issue.
It called on the monarch to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London.
Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade that enriched their ancestors, but like the UK government have not issued an official apology for the slave trade.
The palace said discussions about the colonial legacy and the slave trade were “important” but “primarily matters for governments to address”.

On a 2022 Caribbean tour, Charles’s son Prince William and his wife, Catherine, were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for slavery reparations. Charles’s younger brother, Prince Edward, later that year cancelled a visit to Grenada after pro-republican protests there.
In Antigua and Barbuda, the royals will attend a parade to mark 45 years of independence.
Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, is a republic and Charles will make a state visit on the 60th anniversary of its independence from Britain.
The trip will feature plenty of meetings with local people and will focus on “the vibrant present and promising future of each country”, the palace said.
The programme includes meetings with cricketing legends in Antigua and Barbuda, where the West Indies team is based, and meeting conservationists responsible for Guyana’s rainforest.

articles.title: Legal battles mount over the off-reserve Millennium Scoop
articles.summary: Courts countrywide are grappling with the complex question of whether federal and provincial governments can be sued for the stark overrepresentation of Indigenous children in the off-reserve child…

image.caption: The Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa. (Benoit Roussel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Indigenous

Courts countrywide are grappling with the complex question of whether federal and provincial governments can be sued for the stark overrepresentation of Indigenous children in the off-reserve child welfare system, delivering dizzyingly mixed results.
Ontario court decision's statements on child welfare system called 'highly problematic'
No one disputes it: the statistics are stark. About eight per cent of the kids in Canada are Indigenous, yet more than half of the children in Canada's child welfare system are Indigenous.
But can federal and provincial governments be sued for the overrepresentation of Indigenous kids in the off-reserve child welfare system?
That's the dispute now unfolding in courts countrywide — with mixed results.

For its part the federal government says no, and British Columbia's top court recently agreed, dismissing a claim against Canada just as lawyers for Indigenous youth in Ontario prepared to appeal a lower court decision they argue "will be a stain on this province’s history" if allowed to stand.
"It's wrong in law, it's wrong on the facts and it's wrong in policy," said David Sterns of Sotos LLP.

In that case, brought by plaintiffs named only as B.M. and C.A., the judge dismissed a lawsuit against Canada and Ontario, saying the overrepresentation of Indigenous kids in the province's system "does not itself convey wrongful state conduct" and instead "may equally demonstrate a high level of care rather than any harmful treatment of the proposed class members."

"The policies in issue in the present claim, although called the 'Millennial Scoop' by the plaintiffs, do not repeat the oppressions of a past era," wrote Ontario Superior Court Justice Edward Morgan.

The ruling got First Nations leaders' attention, prompting the Anishinabek Nation, Chiefs of Ontario and Nishnawbe Aski Nation political organizations to intervene in an appeal heard this week in Toronto.
"That reasoning, in my view, is very highly problematic and very dangerous," said Linda Debassige, grand council chief of the Anishinabek Nation, which advocates for 39 communities.

"It's to me in the same light that Indian residential school denialism exists. It's a dangerous pathway to limit the availability of justice for First Nations children and families, specifically, in this setting. The oppression is real. It still exists."
Some advocates call the ongoing mass removal of Indigenous kids from their families the Millenium Scoop, connecting today's child welfare system to residential schools and the Sixties Scoop.
Proposed lead plaintiffs B.M. and C.A. are First Nations and Inuit respectively, and their lawyers' appeal filings call the judge's reasoning misguided and patronizing.
1 case among many
In its appeal argument, Canada says it "acknowledges the important societal concerns raised" but maintains these are complex policy issues that lay outside judges' expertise.
"The claim is not grounded in any specific law or policy, but rather it seeks to subject to judicial scrutiny the entire provincial child welfare system," Canada argues.

items: Chief says Canada blocking effort to take back control of child and family services
Carney government files 3rd court challenge in First Nations child welfare complaint

blocks.text: A proactively disclosed May 2025 federal briefing note says, "Consistent with its belief that we all have a role to play in reconciliation, Canada has taken the position that some claims against Canada should be dismissed, given the provincial control over child welfare."
Debassige denounced such talk as "Canada just wiping their hands clean" to create a "jurisdictional pinball vacuum."

The Ontario appeal joins a complex constellation of cases filed after Ottawa agreed to a $23.4-billion settlement with First Nations children and families harmed in the on-reserve child welfare system.

That settlement stemmed from a landmark 2016 Canadian Human Rights Tribunal finding that Canada racially discriminated against First Nations youth on-reserve and in Yukon by chronically underfunding child and family services.

items: Judge approves historic $23B First Nations child welfare compensation agreement
First Nations sue Canada over child-welfare system's destruction of culture, language

blocks.text: Youth living off-reserve when apprehended are not included, however, and their lawyers are getting dizzyingly uneven results.

Last year, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed a proposed national class action, the Stonechild case, because Canada was the only defendant and provinces were excluded. Lawyers are seeking leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Since then, child welfare survivors filed lawsuits in six provinces.

A claim in Quebec was authorized to proceed. Manitoba consented for a case to proceed. The B.C. Court of Appeal late last month dismissed a claim against Canada but allowed a lawsuit against B.C. to proceed.
Factor in the Ontario case, and the jumble of inconsistent outcomes means Canada's top court may have to weigh in, said Sterns.
"We think that Canada needs to remain in the case. They are a necessary party," he said.
"They have a lot to answer for when it comes to Indigenous child welfare, both on and off reserve, and we think this is an issue that is ripe to be decided by the Supreme Court of Canada."
As for Ontario, the province said on appeal it recognizes the deeply felt impacts experienced by Indigenous children and families but still opposes the lawsuit.
"This proposed class action is a sweeping inquiry into the child welfare, health care and education sectors in Ontario," the filing says.
Ontario calls the claims "imprecise," comprising many thousands of unique interactions with independently suable Children's Aid Societies.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.

articles.title: Brooke Eby, TikToker who used wit and sincerity to educate people about her life with ALS, dead at 37
articles.summary: Brooke Eby, a U.S. woman who shared her diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, with honesty and humour, amassing millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, has died of the disease at 37.

image.caption: Brooke Eby, shown in a photo posted in March 2024, was known for her TikTok and Instagram posts under the handle @limpbroozkit, detailing her life with ALS. Eby died Thursday at 37. (@limpbroozkit/Instagram)

blocks.text: World·New
Brooke Eby, a U.S. woman who shared her diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, with honesty and humour, amassing millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, has died of the disease at 37.
Maryland woman amassed millions of views documenting her diagnosis and life with ALS

"Millions came to know Brooke through her social media presence, where she offered an unfiltered window into living with ALS," the ALS Network wrote in a tribute Thursday, the day of Eby's death. "She could explain a devastating reality, challenge a misconception, and make people laugh, sometimes all in the same post."

Eby first realized she had a health problem at age 29, developing a limp on her left side that she initially assumed was an exercise injury. It took years of testing before she was definitively diagnosed in 2022 with ALS, sometimes known as Lou Gehrig's disease.

ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that attacks nerve cells in the brain and the spinal cord, resulting in loss of muscle movement, eventually causing paralysis and death. Life expectancy is generally two to five years. There is no cure.

"They tell you that you are going to go paralyzed, you're going to lose the ability to move, to talk, to swallow, to breathe, all of it," Eby explained in one of her most popular videos, telling her story as she applied makeup. "So that day sucked."

Eby said she crawled into bed for two months and ate a pack of M&M's a day, until she attended a friend's wedding as a bridesmaid, using a walker and wearing a bridesmaid dress that was "way too tight because of all the M&M's."
She wanted to leave but a friend said, "Or, we can make this really fun."
Half an hour later the bride was limboing under the walker and Eby was giving people "walker rides" — a turning point in Eby's life that is also one of her earliest posts about her diagnosis.
"That was the point where I was like, 'OK, we gotta live life in dog years here,'" she said. "If I'm going to live two to five years, we've got to make every one of those years worth seven."
A life on full display

In her videos, Eby told jokes, answered questions and detailed her life, including trips to medical clinics, moments with friends and family and the deterioration of her body. In one of her last posts, on Sept. 3, in a wheelchair and with a ventilation mask over her nose, she talks about her difficulty speaking. It's called "Loosh lipsh."
Aside from her social media presence, Eby also worked to help further ALS research.

"Whether she was rallying her community and raising money for ALS organizations, taking us inside the life of someone living with ALS, or starting a peer-to-peer network to help people with ALS and their caregivers better navigate this disease, she poured herself into this cause," Target ALS, a U.S.-based medical research foundation, said in a tribute.

items: Grey's Anatomy star Eric Dane, who went on to be an advocate for ALS awareness, dead at 53
Flames assistant GM Chris Snow dies from ALS complications

blocks.text: Target ALS said in July 2025 that Eby had raised more than $1 million US for ALS research.

"I have ALS at a relatable age," she wrote in People magazine in 2025. "Personally, I always associated this disease with older men. That makes it easier to look away and be like, 'That's not my problem.' But I could be someone’s daughter, sister, mom, girlfriend, wife. I think people see me and it’s a little more real. It’s more like a shock to the system, and then they start caring more.
"My TikTok presence will live on after I die, so I hope it serves as a visual diary for anyone who gets diagnosed and needs a guide."

articles.title: No Canadians elected to world hockey governing body; Turkey, New Zealand represented
articles.summary: Hockey Canada president and chief executive officer Katherine Henderson was up for one of the minimum three female spots on the IIHF council at Friday's election, but was eliminated in the second of…

image.caption: Hockey Canada president and CEO Katherine Henderson was up for one of the minimum three female spots on IIHF council. Hungary, Turkey and Poland secured seats. (Jeff McIntosh/Canadian Press/File)

blocks.text: Hockey·New

Hockey Canada president and chief executive officer Katherine Henderson was up for one of the minimum three female spots on the IIHF council at Friday's election, but was eliminated in the second of three rounds of voting in Tenerife, Spain. That means no Canadians have been elected to the council, a surprising result for a nation considered one of the sport's powerhouses.
Hockey Canada's Katherine Henderson fails to secure 1 of 3 spots for women
No Canadians have been elected to the International Ice Hockey Federation's council, a surprising result for a nation considered one of the sport's powerhouses.

Hockey Canada president and chief executive officer Katherine Henderson was up for one of the minimum three female spots on council at Friday's election at the IIHF's semi-annual congress in Tenerife, Spain.
Henderson was eliminated in the second of three rounds of voting. Hungary's Zsuzsanna Kolbenheyer, Turkey's Merve Tunali and Poland's Marta Zawadzka won the council seats.
Canada will be represented regionally on the council by American Mike Trimboli, who was elected vice-president for the Americas and Oceania after running unopposed.

He replaces former Hockey Canada president and CEO Bob Nicholson, who had held the role since 2012 but did not seek re-election. Former Hockey Canada president Murray Costello served as vice-president for five years before Nicholson took over.
While Canada will not have a member on council, the IIHF will have representation from non-traditional hockey nations, including Tunali, Andy Mills of New Zealand and Aivaz Omorkanov of Kyrgyzstan.
Germany's Franz Reindl was elected to replace outgoing president Luc Tardif, who represents France but was born and raised in Quebec, while Petr Briza of Czechia was re-elected senior vice-president.
Canada had been represented on the IIHF Council since 1978, apart from a four-year gap from 1994-98, when American Walter Bush Jr. held the Americas vice-president position.

articles.title: Palestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hears
articles.summary:
Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol

Palestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab…

blocks.text: Palestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard.

Five defendants are accused by prosecutors of being part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards, so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones.

Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, went on trial at Woolwich crown court on Friday charged with criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024. They deny the charges.

Prosecutor Diana Heer told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring it’s destruction with our brains and muscle.”
Jurors were told that a security guard, Nigel Shaw, who had struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella, suffered a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked.

Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers.

“When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.”
She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am.
The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel.

Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night. It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.”

She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet.

The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught” unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”.
The trial continues.

articles.title: FlyDubai 'hero' pilot speaks for first time
articles.summary: India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Captain Smit Machchhar via video call. Meanwhile, authorities in the UAE and Israel said an investigation is making progress.

image.caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to Captain Smit Machchhar through a video callImage: ANI Video Grab/ANI

blocks.text: The Indian Flydubai pilot who was stabbed by his copilot in an apparent attempt to crash the plane has spoken about his ordeal for the first time.

After being seriously wounded, Captain Smit Machchhar managed unlock the cockpit door. This enabled other passengers to enter the cockpit and restrain the copilot, while a deadheading pilot took control of the aircraft.
"I had so many wounds. I had fallen down," Machchhar told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi via video call from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi.
"I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realized that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives."

blocks.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar is currently hospitalized in Abu DhabiImage: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP

blocks.text: Some 180 passengers were on board the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv which had to be diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, due to the situation. Most passengers were Israeli nationals.

Anwar Gargash, an adviser to the UAE president, took to social media on Friday to say Machchhar deserved "the highest recognition for embodying courage and responsibility in the face of a terrorist act and an imminent catastrophe," all while calling him a "true hero."
The suspected attacker, an Omani national, was arrested upon landing in Saudi Arabia, with the motive still being unclear, with Israel saying it believes it was an attempted Islamist attack.
Official labels incident 'terrorist act'
A senior official from the United Arab Emirates on Friday labeled the incident as a terrorist attack. Israel used similar terms to describe the incident.
FlyDubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith said the company will carry out a full investigation of the incident.
"It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts," he said in a statement.
The company said it will suspend its flights to Tel Aviv until October 15 at least.
Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt
Israeli officials to investigate suspect: report

A source also told Reuters that Israeli officials are expected to investigate the flight's co-pilot, currently held in the UAE. The source emphasized it was the UAE who's responsible for the investigation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country was looking into whether the co-pilot had been instructed by anyone.
"Whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price, Netanyahu said.

Many Israelis were stranded in the UAE as a result of the flight suspension between the two countries following the incident, with Israeli airlines receiving the necessary approvals to start repatriating Israeli nationals back to Israel.

articles.title: CBS Sports describes Tony Romo's permanent exit as mutual parting
articles.summary: CBS Sports and Tony Romo have officially parted ways, one month after the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback pleaded no contest to charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated.

image.caption: CBS broadcaster Tony Romo, left, pleaded no contest to charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated earlier this year. He had been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017. (Adrian Kraus/Associated Press/File)

blocks.text: NFL
CBS Sports and Tony Romo have officially parted ways, one month after the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback pleaded no contest to charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated.
Ex-NFL QB pleaded no contest to DWI charge after July traffic stop in Wisconsin
Romo had been on leave since his July 23 arrest in Wisconsin. He had been the lead game analyst for CBS' NFL coverage since 2017.

"CBS Sports and Tony Romo have mutually agreed to part ways," CBS Sports said Friday in a statement. "We thank Tony for his contributions over the past nine years and wish him the best moving forward."

Analyst JJ Watt had joined play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson on CBS Sports' lead NFL team during Romo's absence. Watt will continue in that role now and all other CBS teams will remain the same.

"I'm proud of what I accomplished at CBS Sports over the last nine years," Romo said in a statement. "I approached my role as a game analyst the way I've approached everything in my life, with a desire to win and be the best that I can be.

"I'm going to use this time to take a break, something I've never done before, and focus on my health and my family before moving on to my next opportunity. I am grateful for my time with CBS Sports and for the continued support of my family and friends, as well as the NFL community and fans."

Romo was arrested following a traffic stop as he was driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. He pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated on Sept. 1 and issued a statement apologizing for the actions that led to his arrest.

items: Romo arrested on suspicion of operating a vehicle while under the influence
More football coverage

blocks.text: According to Milwaukee County court records, Romo lost his driving privileges for six months and was ordered to complete an alcohol assessment program.

"The past month has been difficult, but it has also been personally significant," Romo said Sept. 1 in a statement on Instagram. "It has required me to confront and own my mistakes fully — to the Lord, to myself, to my family and now to the public."

Romo said the multiple back surgeries that led to his retirement as a player "left me with constant, debilitating pain." He noted that the pain "led to a dependence on pain medication, and my efforts to get off those medications led to an over-reliance on alcohol."
"None of this is an excuse," Romo said. "These are my failures and I take responsibility for them."
Romo said he is working with a team of doctors to address his health and "make the necessary changes."
The 46-year-old Romo made four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004-16 and was spent entirely with Dallas.
