articles.title: Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election
articles.summary:
Guarantee will remain until 2030, but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says

Andy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said.
The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.
In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.
In his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.
However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes.
It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.
The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050.

However, the Resolution Foundation thinktank said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.
Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.
“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.
“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”

Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.
Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care reform would be “electoral suicide”.
However, YouGov has published polling suggesting that voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.
In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he would end the pension triple lock and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.
Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

articles.title: Spain's parliament rejects housing bill as protests continue
articles.summary: Spain's minority government suffered defeat in parliament as it tried to push through a pair of emergency measures aimed at making housing more affordable. A pensioner's eviction and protests led to…

image.caption: Parliamentarians voted with a crowd of protesters outside awaiting the resultsImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Spain's parliament has narrowly voted down a pair of emergency government decrees aiming to quell widespread protests against rising rental costs for housing.

Hundreds of protesters were gathered outside the parliament in Madrid amid the marathon debate culminating in a pair of votes on Friday. They yelled "shame" and "your profits, our misery," as news of the measures being quashed filtered through.

Spain has been gripped by protests for around a week, including a tent city set up in central Madrid, ignited by the eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment that threw the more longstanding issue of unaffordable housing costs into sharp focus.
Why and how did the emergency decrees fail?
Left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority government in Spain and so relies on opposition support to legislate.
Sanchez spoke at the close of a marathon 5-hour debate in the Chamber of Deputies ahead of the vote, urging members: "Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think."

blocks.caption: Sanchez tried to rally majority support for the measures at the last in parliament, but could not succeed Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One Catalan party that sometimes supports Sanchez's government, the economically right-leaning Junts group, joined the opposition in voting down the measures.

The first emergency decree, which the government said would stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder and provide tax incentives to encourage renting, failed by a narrow margin of 178-172.
The second decree, which sought to make residential leases automatically renewable by tenants, fell further short of a majority at 184-166.
Opponents to the measures argued, among other things, that they risked compounding the situation by reducing housing supply.
Some also argued that Sanchez should respond to the deadlock by calling early elections, possibly initiating a wholesale change of government.

blocks.caption: Rising rents were a sensitive issue in Spain for years, but one particularly emotive eviction brought it to the boilImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did protesters say after the vote?
The Tenants' Union which had led protests across Spain said it would press on with plans for more mass rallies on Saturday, aiming to continue heaping pressure on the coalition and opposition alike.
"The encampment will continue and will continue expanding to other neighborhoods," Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Rio said. "We're aiming for a general strike."

The current wave of protests, albeit concerning an issue that's been bubbling away near the surface for years, was triggered by the high-profile eviction of 87-year-old Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment she had occupied for almost all of her life.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen Abascal has since been granted a reprieve, but the more widespread attempts to improve the situation remain stalled for nowImage: Francesco Militello Mirto/IPA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How tough is Spain's housing market?
The investment company owning Abascal's building reversed the measure in her case this week but only after the issue had become a symbol of growing frustration of housing costs.

Rents have roughly doubled in Spain in the last decade and young people, facing one of Europe's toughest labor markets for school-leavers and graduates, frequently live with their parents past the age of 30.

"People have said 'enough is enough;' this ⁠cannot ​go on. The housing problem must be resolved; structural measures must be taken, and this cannot ​continue," Abascal's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview with Reuters on Thursday.

The next step after Friday's failed vote in parliament is difficult to identify. Sanchez has so far ruled out calling early elections. He could try to formulate another emergency decree or decrees in response to the protests, but any such move would need to overcome the same hurdles in parliament.

articles.title: Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows
articles.summary:
Opposition lawmakers joined forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old

Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have joined forces to reject emergency…

blocks.text: Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have joined forces to reject emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against the widespread protest movement that has swelled in recent days.

As protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against a package of decrees by Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.

The long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.

On Friday, as a new poll suggested that two-thirds of people in Spain support the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mulling whether to bring forward next year’s elections, potentially to this November.

Late on Thursday, as news broke of that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties.

blocks.caption: A sprawling protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, where demonstrators are demanding affordable housing.  Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: For many, Abascal’s eviction was a tipping point for feelings about Spain’s housing market, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, resulting in significant hardship for many.
Earlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain said the average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month – an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s.

The protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past.
after newsletter promotion

The government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing.

“They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.”

Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then, the encampment had swelled to more than 1,500 tents – a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space.
Such demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta.
As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, one protester, Marta García, said: “People here are disappointed. We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.”

articles.title: Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
articles.summary: More than 550 schools have been disrupted as protests over standards and lack of teachers continue.

blocks.text: On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
In Marseille, fireworks were thrown at police and teachers were also inadvertently splashed with petrol at a school there, officials said.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes had suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government.

"We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of who were children - had been taken into custody.
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."

articles.title: P7.2T budget for 2027 includes El Niño preparedness measures --House leader
articles.summary: The chairperson of the House committee on appropriations assured that the House of Representatives will approve an “El Niño-ready” budget for 2027, amid forecasts of worsening dry conditions.

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 12:11am
The chairperson of the House committee on appropriations assured that the House of Representatives will approve an “El Niño-ready” budget for 2027, amid forecasts of worsening dry conditions.
PAGASA earlier said a strong El Niño is already active and could intensify into a very strong El Niño by late 2026.
"It was the commitment of the House to make sure that the 2027 national budget is El Niño-ready," Rep. Mikaela Suansing of the first district of Nueva Ecija said in an online interview Friday.

The committee's Budget Amendments Review Sub Committee (BARSC) on Thursday recommended several amendments to the proposed P7.2 trillion 2027 national budget to prepare the country for the "very strong" El Niño that is expected to persist until early 2027.
Among the amendments are the P150 million for the Agricultural Transport and Support Infrastructure Project.

"This would be the cable car systems, which will be much cheaper for high-value crops being planted in the mountainous areas. So rather than building costly farm-to-market roads, this will be trams that will transport goods from one mountain to another, which will be much cheaper and more economical for our systems in high-value crops," House committee on agriculture and food head Rep. Mark Enverga said.

"Ang ganda ng programang ito kasi yung una niyang tinutugunan, yung sitwasyon ng vegetable farmers natin sa Benguet. Earlier this year, ang nangyari, yung mga kamatis, yung mga repolyo, dahil hindi nila maibaba, tinapon na lang nila sa kalsada," Suansing said.

"I believe this is not the first of its kind. There are already existing trams and monorails in some parts of the country in vegetable-growing regions in the highlands. But this one is additional, and the Department of Agriculture will improve the system," she added.
The BARSC also recommended an additional P500 million for the Expanded Fertilizer Assistance Program.
The program has already been allocated more than P14 billion under the proposed 2027 National Expenditures Program.
An additional P125 million for the Department of Agriculture and P4 billion were also recommended for solar pumps for irrigation.
The BARSC also recommended a total of P105 million for hybrid solar-powered ice plants.
Although P16 billion has already been included in the 2027 NEP for farm-to-market roads, the BARSC recommended an additional P4.96 billion.
The BARSC also recommended an additional P10 billion for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk.
The BARSC also discussed crops that rice farmers can plant when El Niño hits the country, including ube.
The 2027 budget earmarks P1.7 billion for high-value crops. The BARSC recommended allotting P100 million specifically for the country's ube industry.
The subcommittee also pitched additional funding of P275 million for UP Project Noah.
The BARSC recommended a total of P116.32 billion worth of amendments in the proposed 2027 national budget.

When asked where the BARSC will source the funds, Suansing replied, "At the moment, we are currently looking through all the programs across all the different agencies. Meron kaming mga batayan na gagamitin para i-identify aling mga programa ang puwede nating makaltasan."
Suansing said the House may approve the budget on October 7. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Woman at centre of Cornell rape inquiry was 'failed' by officials, says New York governor
articles.summary: The woman, known as Jane Doe, alleges she was raped by seven students at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.

blocks.text: New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape case was "failed" at "every turn".
The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024.
The case was investigated at the time but no charges were laid. It recently reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She has now appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead it.
This appointment was made after Hochul said she "lost faith" in the local prosecutor's ability to oversee the investigation.
Expressing outrage that local prosecutors did not interview the accuser themselves, Hochul on Friday said Doe was "failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her".
She has also vowed to close a "loophole" that prevents prosecutors from pursuing rape charges in cases when the victim has voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol.
"If someone is too intoxicated to consent it should not matter if they chose to use drugs or alcohol," said Hochul, adding: "Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for gang rape."
James appeared alongside Hochul at Friday's news conference, pledging to "lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
She said her office would interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted.

District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who previously led the investigation, has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.

Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.
