articles.title: Loren may rejoin Senate majority – spokesman
articles.summary: The camp of Sen. Loren Legarda is not ruling out the possibility of the lawmaker returning to the country and joining the majority bloc, saying shifting alliances is a regular feature of the upper…

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The camp of Sen. Loren Legarda is not ruling out the possibility of the lawmaker returning to the country and joining the majority bloc, saying shifting alliances is a regular feature of the upper chamber’s fluid politics.

“I will not rule that out. In the last four years there have been four Senate presidents. The majority has changed the last four years so I wouldn’t rule that out. It’s apparently a normal thing in the Senate,” Legarda’s spokesman Tony La Viña told One News yesterday.
He added that it would be natural for Legarda to maintain open lines with her peers, given her standing in the Senate.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if she does that. I’m also not surprised if she’s talking to other senators because she’s a good senator, she’s very good with her colleagues, they actually love her, I will say that almost universally,” he added.

Asked whether Legarda’s departure from the Senate was a strategic bargaining chip for the administration to woo her back to its fold, La Viña said ongoing impeachment proceedings were distinct and instead pointed to the political fallout from corruption allegations raised against her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste.

“I wouldn’t know that, you can also say otherwise that the charges are … but she actually doesn’t think that this has something to do with the impeachment because she knows Senate politics and it’s kinda…it can move any hour, any day,” La Viña explained.
“We actually think this is really about Leandro Leviste’s exposé on corruption, that’s the one that upset a lot of people and so that’s just politics,” he added.

Since Aug. 3, Legarda has been on medical leave from the Senate and was reportedly in France receiving treatment. Her latest extension of leave is valid until Oct. 9, making her absent from the chamber for two full months.
Her absence is among the reasons senators voted to adjust the voting denominator set by impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero.
Legarda’s prolonged absence also coincides with the Office of the Ombudsman’s plunder investigation into the senator and her son over the alleged multibillion-peso solar energy anomaly.

articles.title: House panel OKs additional P1.95 billion for school safety
articles.summary: The House committee on appropriations’ budget amendments review subcommittee (BARSc) has approved the Department of Education (DepEd)’s requested P1.952-billion additional funding for…

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
Security officials at Ramon Magsaysay High School in Cubao, Quezon City inspect students’ bags before they enter the premises on August 24, 2026.
Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The House committee on appropriations’ budget amendments review subcommittee (BARSc) has approved the Department of Education (DepEd)’s requested P1.952-billion additional funding for school safety and other unfunded programs.

Of the additional funds, P952 million will be for the Basic Education Facilities Fund to construct classrooms; P500 million for the School Safety and Security Program; P350 million for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program; P75 million for Special Needs Education; P50 million for Madrasah Education and P25 million for Indigenous Peoples Education.
DepEd was previously allocated P975.96 billion in the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
DepEd said the P350-million boost for the ARAL Program will sustain tutoring and remediation for targeted learners nationwide.
During School Year 2025-2026, targeted recovery interventions helped reduce the number of struggling readers nationwide from 6.7 million to 2.2 million.

The government has proposed P11.03 billion for the Department of Labor and Employment’s Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged Workers program in 2027, targeting 672,776 disadvantaged and displaced workers nationwide.
The proposed outlay is maintained at the 2026 NEP level.
Budget watchdog access denied
Budget watchdogs seeking to monitor the House's review of amendments to the national budget said they were denied access to BARSc proceedings.

“These executive meetings have historically been the avenue to make congressional insertions in the national budget,” Tim Salomon of the Caucus of Development Non-Government Organizations Network told The STAR.
People’s Budget Coalition said civil society organizations and member of the media were not allowed to monitor the BARSc proceedings onsite. — Christine Boton, Aubrey Rose Inosante

articles.title: Suspension of China exports to drive up fuel prices
articles.summary: Fuel prices are seen to rise in October after China announced that it will suspend its exports of refined products to the Asia-Pacific region, according to the Department of Energy.

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
Gasoline attendants fill up vehicles of customers including some public utility vehicles at a station in Quezon City on April 13, 2026.
STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Fuel prices are seen to rise in October after China announced that it will suspend its exports of refined products to the Asia-Pacific region, according to the Department of Energy.

“Bad news, somehow, is that China announced that it will temporarily suspend its exports of refined products to Asia-Pacific buyers. This is no longer crude oil tightness. This will be a refined product with tightness because China is a big refining country,” DOE Oil Industry Management Bureau director Rino Abad yesterday told radio dzBB.

Abad said that the decision by China may create “refined products tightness” as other countries will need to either increase their output or seek more distant markets, which will add costs and drive up retail prices.

“We can’t predict the situation this October yet. If possible, there are still many countries outside the region that we can source from, such as the US, Canada and Australia. But this could have an impact on prices,” he said.
Meanwhile, gasoline and diesel prices are expected to move in opposite directions next week amid continued market volatility spurred by the Middle East crisis.
Following four days of trading in the regional benchmark Mean of Platts Singapore, industry estimates point to a looming increase of P1.50 to P1.80 per liter in gasoline prices.
Diesel prices, on the other hand, are likely to go down by P0.50 to P0.80 per liter.
The projections may still change depending on the final trading day of the week, with the official price adjustments to be announced on Oct. 5.
“Lingering supply stability concerns have resulted in oil’s volatile movement this week,” Jetti Petroleum president Leo Bellas told reporters yesterday.
While supplies from the Middle East recovered, Bellas said renewed concerns over potential disruptions following stalled US-Iran peace talks exerted upward pressure on prices.

Prices also jumped on fears of worsening global product shortages after China suspended exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau. This added pressure to already strained product markets following refinery damage in the Middle East and Russia.
“Oil surged further following reports of more US troops moving to the Middle East and resumption of attacks on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections,” Bellas added.
This week, the DOE prescribed minimum price cuts of P0.24 per liter for gasoline, P7.57 for diesel and P5.85 for kerosene.
The rollback reflects easing supply concerns following increased oil flows from Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Impeachment court targets verdict by December 16
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court is eyeing to hand down a final verdict in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte by Dec. 16, running ahead of schedule despite two session cancellations this week.

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am

Senators consult retired Supreme Court Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday, September 16, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court is eyeing to hand down a final verdict in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte by Dec. 16, running ahead of schedule despite two session cancellations this week.

Court spokesman Reginald Tongol announced yesterday that the impeachment court has advanced anywhere from 20 to 27 days ahead of its initial calendar, drastically shortening a process originally expected to drag on until February or March 2027.

Tongol said House prosecutors could finish presenting their evidence for Article II or ill-gotten wealth and potentially conclude their entire case if they drop Article III or bribery by the end of next week.

“Now, with the way the impeachment trial is going on, our impeachment court’s confidence is stronger that this will be finished before Senate goes on holiday recess,” he said in a virtual press briefing.
“So by Dec. 16 we will have a final verdict,” he added.
The accelerated timeline stems from the prosecution panel’s decision to drop several witnesses from their original list.

For Article II, which tackles the Vice President’s alleged unexplained wealth, prosecutors have used eight of their allocated 12 days and have four days left to present their remaining witnesses, which include representatives from banks, insurance firms, the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
Tongol said the prosecution might be done with Article II by Thursday or Friday next week if they decide not to add more witnesses or testimonies.
Once the prosecution rests, they will file a formal offer of documentary exhibits before the defense panel opens its 30-day presentation of evidence, he said.
The court expects the defense to streamline its witness lineup in a similar manner.
Tongol also ruled out scheduling make-up hearings after Oct. 15 to compensate for this week’s cancellations, pointing out that the legislative calendar leaves no room for adjustments.
He noted that senators would devote the upcoming legislative recess to budget deliberations alongside the country’s hosting of the ASEAN Summit.
The impeachment trial will take a recess after Oct. 15 and is slated to resume on Nov. 23.
Evidence review

The defense team defended its granted manifestation to postpone the prosecution’s presentation of its AMLC witness who is expected to testify on the P6.7 billion in transactions linked to the bank accounts of Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa maintained that they needed time to review the documents submitted by the AMLC.

“We are also grateful for the understanding of our presiding officer (Sen. Francis Escudero) because of course we only got the summary… because it’s new and we really need to look into that. There are details there that we feel that we need to look into. So, it’s a really big deal… And we do not deny that we were the ones who requested if we could be given time. Not just for cross-examination,” Poa said at a press conference on Thursday.
The impeachment court canceled its whole-day proceedings for Thursday to give the defense enough time to prepare for the testimony of AMLC executive director Ronel Buenaventura. — Bella Cariaso

articles.title: DFA rejects China claim over waters off Batanes
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs “firmly and strongly” rejected yesterday the Chinese embassy’s assertion that China has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the waters off Batanes.

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Foreign Affairs
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs “firmly and strongly” rejected yesterday the Chinese embassy’s assertion that China has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the waters off Batanes.

In a statement issued after a Chinese research boat was monitored in the area before the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove it away, the DFA emphasized that the foreign vessel was illegally operating within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of the Philippines.
The DFA noted that Chinese research and survey vessel Jia Hai Ke 7 was detected operating approximately 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, Batanes.

“The Department affirms that the Philippine Coast Guard was conducting lawful and routine law enforcement operations in response to a suspected unauthorized Marine Scientific Research (MSR) activity in the waters off Batanes.”

Under Article 246 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the DFA said “marine scientific research in the EEZ and on the continental shelf shall be conducted with the consent of the coastal State.”
“The Philippines did not receive any request from the Chinese side and no consent has been given to any Chinese vessel,” it added.
The DFA gave assurance that the Philippines “will continue to uphold the country’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in its EEZ peacefully and responsibly in accordance with international law.”
China rejects DFA statement
The Chinese embassy in Manila issued its own declaring that it “firmly rejects the statement issued by the DFA.”
“China reiterates that, in accordance with international law, including UNCLOS, China has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the relevant waters,” it argued.

The Chinese embassy said that in accordance with the provisions of UNCLOS Articles 74 and 83, as well as a so-called consensus reached between China and the Philippines, the matter should be properly resolved through negotiations.
It said a PCG vessel “harassed the Chinese scientific research vessel conducting normal operations in waters under China’s jurisdiction.”
“China has taken, and will continue to take, necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests,” the embassy said.
Academic infection
Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. has expressed concern over how China may be trying to influence Filipino students on issues concerning territory and sovereignty.
In a podcast interview with Ray Powell and Jim Carouso, he was asked about a claim by so-called Chinese scholars that Batanes belongs to China.
“I think that’s state-sponsored, the timing was ill-released,” Teodoro said.
He said such narratives are not about political influence but are rather meant “to infect the academic environment.”
He said it is “something I’m extremely concerned with and we are working with the national security in order to scope it out.” — Bella Cariaso

articles.title: NBI invites VP over ex-cop’s cash delivery claim
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will invite Vice President Sara Duterte to answer allegations of dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to…

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
NBI director Melvin Matibag
Edd Gumban / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will invite Vice President Sara Duterte to answer allegations of dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to members of the Duterte family.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said Thursday that the invitation is part of the bureau’s effort to give the Vice President and other people named in Gracioso’s sworn statement an opportunity to respond to the allegations.
“We will ask questions based on what is stated in the affidavit and what has been attributed to them,” Matibag told reporters.
The NBI will also invite Davao City 1st district Rep. Paolo Duterte, former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his wife, Rowena.
Matibag said the bureau wants to hear their denials and other explanations, particularly after some of those named have said they did not know Gracioso.
The NBI chief said the invitation could also become relevant if Gracioso faces a possible perjury complaint.
“If they want to file a perjury case, they need a document to base it on. What document will that be? The affidavit,” Matibag said.
He said the NBI, which took Gracioso’s sworn statement, would be able to certify the original or a certified true copy of the document for use in any legal proceedings.

Gracioso, a dismissed former police officer who said he served as part of Velasco’s security detail, has alleged that he delivered cash-filled suitcases to the Vice President, her brother Paolo and former president Rodrigo Duterte on Velasco’s instructions. He claimed that the deliveries to the Vice President totaled more than P2 billion.
The Vice President has denied knowing Gracioso and receiving money from him, and said her lawyers were awaiting an official copy of his affidavit before pursuing legal action.
The NBI has said Gracioso’s allegations and supporting evidence, including photographs, are still subject to authentication and verification.

articles.title: DENR heightens measures vs El Niño
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources has strengthened its mitigation measures against the ongoing El Niño.

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
UP Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (UPIESM) Assistant Professor Alan Racoma shows the position of the Super El Niño at the Project Noah office, October 1, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources has strengthened its mitigation measures against the ongoing El Niño.

The DENR’s heightened preparations include building additional water sources, promoting water conservation, protecting watersheds and forests, preventing forest fires, safeguarding vulnerable ecosystems and protecting personnel from extreme heat.
El Niño is expected to bring increased risks of prolonged dry conditions, reduced water availability and extreme heat in parts of the country.
“With the critical action window now upon us, every DENR unit must proactively execute climate adaptation and risk reduction protocols,” DENR chief Juan Miguel Cuna said.
Among its measures, the DENR has constructed small water impounding structures and rainwater harvesting systems to provide additional water supply during periods of limited rainfall.

Its regional offices and attached agencies are also strengthening water conservation, watershed monitoring, forest-fire prevention, ecosystem protection and heat-safety measures in coordination with local governments and other stakeholders.

In Central Luzon, Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Office-Pampanga and regional field units are conducting information campaigns in barangays and community colleges in Guagua and Lubao to promote simple water-saving practices such as using buckets instead of hoses, reusing greywater, repairing leaks and harvesting rainwater.

In Caraga, the Mines and Geosciences Bureau advised mining companies and processing plants to manage water demand, check for leaks, harvest rainwater and establish cooling stations and early warning systems for extreme heat. Advisories have also been sent to provincial governors to strengthen local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Councils and monitor critical watersheds.

Meanwhile, the Environmental Management Bureau in the Davao Region has strengthened health and safety measures for field personnel, including limiting high-exposure outdoor work from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., providing personal protective equipment and ensuring continuous hydration.
These measures help secure water for communities during dry periods, protect forests and watersheds and safeguard people and livelihoods that depend on healthy ecosystems.
Water impounding structures and rainwater harvesting systems provide additional sources of water when rainfall is limited, while conservation efforts help make available supplies last longer.
Protecting forests and watersheds also help maintain the natural systems that collect, store and regulate water.
‘Don’t hoard bottled water’
Meanwhile, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), in a statement, assured the public of enough supply of bottled water in the market and urged consumers not to hoard.
“The department will intensify price monitoring and continue to coordinate closely with manufacturers and distributors to ensure a steady supply in the market,” it said.
In addition, the DTI said it would closely monitor and address complaints on overpriced plastic drums, water containers and other related commodities.
“Businesses and sellers are reminded to act responsibly and refrain from taking advantage of the situation through unjustified price increases,” the DTI said.
It also warned businesses selling overpriced items of penalties and sanctions under existing laws. — Louella Desiderio

articles.title: President Marcos inspects PICC ahead of November Asean summit
articles.summary: President Marcos yesterday led a walkthrough of the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City, one of the main venues of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit…

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am

President Marcos inspects the Philippine International Convention Center as preparations continue for the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits, which the Philippines will host as Asean chair on Nov. 16 to 18.
PCO

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos yesterday led a walkthrough of the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City, one of the main venues of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits in Metro Manila from Nov. 16 to 18.
The regional meeting will be held under the theme: “Navigating Our Future, Together.”
According to the Presidential Communications Office, preparations are underway to ensure the Philippines is ready to welcome regional leaders and delegates for these high-level meetings.

On Thursday, the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) joined an inter-agency coordination meeting with the Armed Forces of the Philippines, Metropolitan Manila Development Authority, Department of Tourism and the Department of the Interior and Local Government to coordinate measures to ensure the smooth and safe conduct of the summits.

The measures being done by the Metro Manila Police include increasing police visibility, providing security coverage along routes to be used and conducting intelligence and information monitoring in strategic areas, such as summit venues, hotels, airports and major transport hubs.
“Our preparation is centered on coordination, readiness and rapid response,” NCRPO officer in charge Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano said in a statement yesterday.

Malacañang has declared Nov. 16 to 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila under Proclamation 1447. The three-day work suspension aims to ease traffic congestion and allow the Philippines, as host country, to ensure the safety and security of summit participants.
Several ASEAN-related meetings will also be held in Metro Manila next month, including the 16th ASEAN Maritime Forum on Nov. 17 and the 14th Expanded ASEAN Maritime Forum on Nov. 18.
On Monday, Marcos will appear on singer Gary Valenciano’s podcast, “Unshaken” at 12 p.m. on YouTube and other major podcast platforms. — EJ Macababbad

articles.title: ‘Funds from China, drug lord went to Dutertes’
articles.summary: About P319 million in funds from Chinese government and corporate sources entered businesses and a foundation linked to the Duterte family, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV alleged yesterday,…

blocks.text: October 3, 2026 | 12:00am
Trillanes: Manases firm got P319 million from China

MANILA, Philippines — About P319 million in funds from Chinese government and corporate sources entered businesses and a foundation linked to the Duterte family, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV alleged yesterday, adding that these funds should be examined as part of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte.
At a press conference in San Juan, Trillanes presented what he described as documents and findings of his research team on the Duterte family’s business and financial ties.

He alleged that more than P319 million entered Cale88 Foods Corp., which he linked to the Vice President’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, while another P150 million went to the Tapang at Malasakit Foundation, where Duterte was identified as a member of the board of trustees.

Trillanes also alleged that members of the Duterte family received P181.6 million from businessman and alleged drug lord Sammy Uy between 2011 and 2013. Of the amount, P38.8 million allegedly went to Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte, P51.5 million to Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, P53.2 million to Cielito Avanceña for Veronica Duterte and P15.6 million to former president Rodrigo Duterte.
Trillanes did not present the alleged payments before the Senate impeachment court because he was dropped as a prosecution witness.
The allegations were made as the Senate impeachment court examines Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth and business interests presented under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment.

The impeachment court has ordered banks, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, Bureau of Internal Revenue and other entities to produce financial records involving Duterte, her husband and corporations linked to them.

The court has also been examining corporate records involving GenCorp Industries Inc. Duterte declared GenCorp as a business interest in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth, but Securities and Exchange Commission records presented during the trial did not list her as a direct shareholder or corporate officer.
The SEC said JTC Group of Companies held a 54.99 percent stake in GenCorp, based on its 2025 General Information Sheet.
Palace reacts

Allegations that the Vice President and her husband received millions in remittances from China cannot be dismissed as the country’s sovereignty is at stake, Palace press officer Claire Castro said yesterday.
“If there is sufficient evidence, it should not be ignored,” Castro said, adding that the administration would withhold judgment this time but stressed that Filipinos deserve to know the truth.

For his part, House prosecution adviser and spokesman Ace Barbers said that Trillanes’ latest disclosures deserve serious examination. “He identified a financial trail. And portions of that trail have already been independently corroborated by official records,” he said.
Trillanes may still be called to testify
Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said that Trillanes’ decision to withdraw as a witness in the impeachment trial came as a surprise to the prosecution.

“It was a surprise decision because… we have been discussing the testimony of senator Trillanes for the longest time. We do not really know his personal reasons,” Kapunan told “Storycon” on One News yesterday.

“We respect that decision (to withdraw). But that does not mean that he cannot be recalled by the Senate-judges, by the presiding officer or by the prosecution itself,” she said, adding that there was a timing problem in the issuance of the subpoena.

Senate impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol dismissed claims that Trillanes was unwelcome at the trial, blaming House prosecutors for the subpoena mix-up and adding that the defense could still summon him.
Tongol said Trillanes’ subpoena was ready on Monday, but Rep. Terry Ridon failed to include him when asked who the prosecution would present this week.
‘NBI tried to bring me to Manila’

Former Office of the Vice President personnel Jefry Tupas alleged that the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) tried to bring him to Manila after receiving “verifiable threats” that he would be kidnapped by the Dutertes.

Tupas said that on Sept. 29, “NBI personnel led by Voltaire Rovira II, who is publicly identified as the Special Assistant for Mindanao Concerns, offered security to my family and me, which we politely declined.”
Tupas said that prior to NBI personnel showing up, NBI Director Melvin Matibag personally informed him in a phone call of the alleged kidnapping threat.
Matibag requested to meet with Tupas in Manila. Tupas said he asked for a formal invitation. Instead of a formal invitation, he was sent a subpoena dated Sept. 28.

Tupas claimed he and his family were being intimidated and threatened by the presence of unidentified and suspicious individuals around their homes and workplaces in Mindanao.?Tupas likewise maintained that the threat did not come from the Dutertes but from other parties.

“I am also issuing this statement to publicly address the alleged threat that the Dutertes will have me abducted. This is a claim that is simply unbelievable. I am confident that the Dutertes have no reason to cause me any harm,” he said. — Bella Cariaso, Helen Flores, Diana Lhyd Suelto, Daphne Galvez, Janvic Mateo, Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
articles.summary:
Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown within four months as rising prices put pressure on households and economies

Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency…
articles.byline: Joanna Partridge, Jillian Ambrose and Mark Sweney

blocks.text: Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after coming under pressure from Donald Trump to ease surging fuel prices.

The drawdown of reserves from some of the world’s largest economies will be coordinated by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and will take place within four months, according to France’s president, Emmanuel Macron.
Macron is the current chair of the G7 – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – and he confirmed the move on Friday following a leaders’ video meeting.
Macron said G7 nations wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.

European countries had come under pressure from the White House in recent days to release emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban. Trump has said he is considering stopping diesel exports to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November.
Macron said G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.

He added that G7 leaders had agreed to make production more flexible so refineries can work at their maximum capacity, and that they would not take any measures to “restrict the exchange of energy and petroleum products between partner countries”.

“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.
The G7 leaders said they would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.

A US export ban would have presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries, but relies on imports to make up the shortfall. Oil analysts had also raised concerns that competition for diesel cargoes on the global market would push prices even higher.

The average price of diesel climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on UK forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists. The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.
Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”
The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.
after newsletter promotion

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that he welcomed the release of more reserves: “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked diesel oil. The process will begin immediately.”
However, Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said release of the reserves would not address the underlying problem in the US.
“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.
“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.

The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started.

articles.title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard speaks out about death of her ex-fiancé, Ken Urker
articles.summary: Gypsy Rose Blanchard, who spent more than seven years in prison for her mother's murder, is speaking out after Ken Urker, her former fiancé and the father of her daughter, died yesterday.

image.caption: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's reintegration into society after serving time in prison was the subject of a documentary series on the Lifetime channel. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Gypsy Rose Blanchard, who spent more than seven years in prison for her mother's murder, is speaking out after Ken Urker, her former fiancé and the father of her daughter, died yesterday.
Urker, 34, was found unresponsive in his Louisiana home on his birthday
Gypsy Rose Blanchard, who spent more than seven years in prison for her mother's murder, is speaking out after her former fiancé and the father of her daughter was found dead on Thursday.
Ken Urker was 34.
He was found unresponsive in his Raceland, La., home on Oct. 1, his birthday.
The Lafourche Parish Sheriff’s Department told CBC News it is still investigating his death, and at this point in the investigation, it has found no evidence of foul play.
Blanchard, speaking exclusively to People and TMZ, said an unidentified substance was found at the scene, and she believes Urker died of an overdose. Police have not confirmed the cause of death.
I don’t know if it was intentional or not," Blanchard told People. "He was not in a good state of mind lately."
She also told the publication that
Urker was the subject of intense scrutiny and cyber-bullying throughout their relationship.

"I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline and every comment," she told People.
Rocky road to love
Blanchard and Urker connected in 2017, when he wrote to her in prison after watching the HBO Documentary Mommy Dead and Dearest.

The film explains how Blanchard's mother, Dee Dee, was believed to have factitious disorder imposed on another (FDIA) — formerly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy — and for years allegedly forced her daughter to use a wheelchair and feeding tubes she didn't need.
In her early 20's, Blanchard and then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn came up with a scheme to murder Dee Dee.
Godejohn is serving a life sentence for first-degree murder.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, and was still incarcerated when Urker proposed to her in October 2018. They briefly called off their engagement, before reuniting in 2019.

Blanchard and Urker separated again for several years, during which time she married Ryan Anderson, and then publicly separated from him in December 2023, four months after she was released from prison.
New beginnings and reality TV
In June 2024, the docuseries Gypsy Rose: Life After Lock Up premiered on the Lifetime channel.
It followed Blanchard as she reintegrated into society, finalized her divorce from Ryan Anderson and rekindled her relationship with Urker.
Blanchard and Urker had a baby together in December 2024, a daughter named Aurora Rain Urker.
Following his death, Blanchard told People that Urker was a devoted parent and the love of her life.
"Ken was an amazing father and a man who was deeply loved. He will forever be my soulmate and my red string, a connection that time, distance and even death can never erase."

Blanchard appeared on the We Need to Talk podcast in June of this year, where she talked about her tumultuous childhood, revisited the night her mother was killed and how she's trying to move past her dark history.
CBC News has reached out to one of Blanchard's former representatives for further comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: "NAZA": Israeli military issues statement on film
articles.summary: The award-winning documentary "NAZA" continues to spark controversy in Israel. The Israeli military has now published a multi-page statement calling the film's portrayal "distorted."

image.caption: Still from the documentary "NAZA"Image: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: When it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in mid-September, "NAZA" received a 25-minute-long standing ovation and the Special Jury Prize. But in Israel, the documentary has fueled heated debate.

Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar described the work of filmmakers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham "treason against the state" and urged that their citizenship be revoked. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also sharply criticized the documentary.

Now the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has also rejected the film's allegations about its conduct during the war in Gaza. In a multi-page document, the military accuses the filmmakers of presenting a "distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture." The film, it says, is based on "substantial factual errors" resulting from "manipulative misrepresentations of reality."
An insider's look at the war

The 80-minute documentary examines the Israel Defense Forces' operations during the war in Gaza. It is based on interviews conducted with 24 anonymous military and intelligence personnel, who describe internal procedures and decision-making processes involved in selecting targets in the Gaza Strip. According to the interviewees, high civilian casualty estimates were, in some cases, deliberately factored into these decisions.

The IDF rejects those claims. It says it has never planned or carried out attacks while anticipating hundreds of civilian deaths. It also disputes the film's claim that artificial intelligence selected targets without human oversight, saying people have always made decisions about targets and attacks.

The military also accuses the filmmakers of omitting important facts. According to the IDF, the film fails to show the role of military legal advisors and commanders in reviewing and authorizing attacks or the measures it says it takes to protect civilians. It also argues that the film does not adequately address the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, in which over 1,200 people were killed and 250 people were taken hostage.

Several human rights organizations and a UN commission have accused Israel of committing acts of genocide in Gaza. According to health authorities in Gaza and other sources, at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began.
'NAZA' opens in theaters worldwide

Speaking at the awards ceremony in Venice in mid-September, co-director Yuval Abraham said: "We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist. That is why it's really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film."
Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham also worked on the film "No Other Land," which won an Oscar for Best Documentary Feature in 2025.
Israeli leaders condemn acclaimed Gaza documentary 'NAZA'

"NAZA" comes from the Hebrew term "Nezek Agavi," meaning collateral damage. According to a soldier interviewed in the film, the acronym is used within the military to refer to the estimated number of civilians who could be killed in an attack.

Numerous human rights organizations, including the Israeli group B'Tselem, have expressed their support for the filmmakers. After its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival, "NAZA" is now showing in theaters worldwide.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Israel's top court allows Arab parties to run in election
articles.summary: The ruling overturns a move by the Central Elections Committee to ban four parties. The conservative Muslim Ra'am party could serve as the kingmaker following the next elections.

image.caption: Israel's top court made a decision that has a massive impact on the upcoming parliamentary election Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israel's Supreme Court on Friday said that four Arab parties may compete in the Israeli parliamentary elections at the end of this month. Arabs make up around one fifth of Israel's population.
The decision overturns a move by the Central Elections Committee (CEC) in late September to ban the Arab parties. The CEC also sought to bar several individual candidates from the race.
What did the Supreme Court decide?

The Court's decision means the United Arab List party, commonly known as Ra'am, and the Joint List, consisting of the Hadash, Balad and Ta'al parties, may run in the parliamentary vote on October 27. The decisions regarding Ra'am and the Joint List were unanimous.
Moreover, the court also overturned a decision to bar Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif from running. Two of the nine judges, however, opposed this decision, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported.

blocks.caption: A protest was held in front of the Israeli Supreme Court on Thursday against the barring of Arab voices in the electionImage: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, the leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party, Sami Abu Shehadeh, was advised by the Supreme Court to voluntarily drop out. The court motioned to Shehadeh that it would uphold the CEC ban on his candidacy.
In an article Shehadeh wrote one day after the Hamas terror attack of October 7, 2023, Shehadeh referred to the attack as "an important historical event."
Hamas-led militants killed around 1,200 people in Israel and abducted more than 250 people.
According to the Times of Israel, Shehadeh told the top court he expressed regret over the article and said he condemned the October 7 attack.

"The same Central Election Committee that disqualified me for an article refused to disqualify all the extreme right-wing racist politicians with all the serious files that were against them," Shehadeh told ​Reuters on Friday.
He added: "Committing a genocide is considered ⁠acceptable and legitimate, but talking about ending the occupation [of Palestinian land] and peace is considered illegitimate."
Israel has repeatedly rejected accusations of genocide in the Palestinian territories.
Why had the CEC decided to ban the Arab parties?
The Central Elections Committee is controlled by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, which consists of right-wing and far-right parties.

According to the Israeli Knesset's basic law, candidates or parties can be barred from elections to the Knesset if they engage in the "negation of the existence of the existence of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state" or "incitement to racism."
The basic law also bars those who show "support for armed struggle by a hostile state or a terrorist organization against the State of Israel."

Parties such as Netanyahu's right-wing Likud or far-right coalition partner Otzma Yehudit have put forward petitions which say Arab parties or various candidates are involved in those aforementioned actions as laid out by the basic law and should be barred.
Ben-Gvir Gaza comments trigger condemnation

The CEC, however, has not pushed to bar controversial lawmakers like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and his Otzma Yehudi party. Ben-Gvir, for example, claimed in 2023 that Jewish rights outweigh those of Palestinians in the West Bank, drawing condemnation from both the US and EU at the time. He has made many controversial statements and actions since then.
How will the top court's decision impact the upcoming election and coalition talks?
The decision by Israel's top court will have a massive impact in the upcoming parliamentary election, as Netanyahu seeks another term as prime minister.
Recent polls show Netanyahu's Likud party in a close race for the most votes with Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli general who leads the Yashar faction.

blocks.caption: Mansour Abbas of the Ra'am Party served in the previous Israeli government [FILE: June 13, 2021]Image: Ariel Schalit/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, neither side will likely garner enough votes to form a government by themselves, meaning that coalition talks will need to be held.
The conservative Ra'am party, led by Mansour Abbas, could be the kingmaker in the coalition talks following the vote.

articles.title: Aviation security back in spotlight after nightmare on flydubai flight to Israel
articles.summary:
Questions raised over cockpit locks and screening of pilots as UAE investigates details and motives of near disaster

At around 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her…

blocks.text: At around 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter Nina to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.

Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he didn’t react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.

Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.
Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”
Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.

As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in around a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.

Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.
In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.
The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”

For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.

In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.

Experts said there had been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.

In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.

Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.

“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”

blocks.caption: People disembark from a flydubai plane carrying Israeli passengers from the disrupted flight at Ben Gurion international airport near Tel Aviv. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive end with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.

Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.

“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane is the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”

There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.

blocks.caption: A passenger with blood on his T-shirt onboard the flydubai plane. Photograph: Amit Segal

blocks.text: There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.
Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”

Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.

The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.

Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.

Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

articles.title: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
articles.summary: The defeat raises pressure on Sánchez to call a snap election, after a series of scandals affecting his party and allies.

blocks.text: Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.
Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.
The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.
Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.

The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.
Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.

The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".
Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas.

The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.
"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".
He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".
Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.

"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.
"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."
However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.
She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."
The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.
Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

articles.title: Intensified Russian strikes are tearing Kyiv apart, warns mayor
articles.summary: Vitaliy Klitschko says Ukraine's capital is in a "very dramatic situation" as Russia hits critical infrastructure.

blocks.text: "We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials.
Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it".
The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days.
The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv.
All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges.
Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network.
One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.
In a published excerpt from his interview to the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings.
"They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."
Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after his Thursday's wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

articles.title: G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil, including diesel, amid energy crunch

image.caption: A diesel pump is seen at a gas station as a person fills up their car in Montreal on April 9, 2026. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

The release would begin immediately and take four months, starting with a "substantial" diesel release within the first 20 days. Diesel prices have soared globally due to the oil supply crunch brought on by fighting in the Middle East between the U.S. and Iran.
Move would start with 'substantial' diesel release within first 20 days
The G7 nations said they agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil, starting with "substantial" amounts of diesel, after the fuel recently hit record prices in the United States.
U.S. President Donald Trump — facing pressure to address surging prices ahead of November's midterm elections — also announced the action on Friday on social media.
"Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately," Trump posted on Truth Social.
The president faces lagging approval ratings as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods.

Gas and diesel prices have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. Trump has insisted prices will come down after the war, though there's no end in sight.
The average price of diesel in Canada was $2.63 per litre as of Thursday, though prices were higher in some cities, like Vancouver, where a litre of the fuel cost about $2.71.

items: The price of diesel is skyrocketing. Here's why Canadians may soon feel it at the grocery store

blocks.text: Trump had a conversation overnight with French President Emmanuel Macron, the chair of the G7, about the need to address rising fuel prices and the availability of petroleum products, according to the French Embassy in the U.S.
Macron on Friday then chaired a video conference of G7 leaders to discuss the issue.

The move also comes after Trump last week floated the idea of banning diesel exports in hopes of bringing down gas prices for American drivers — a move experts caution could backfire, putting strain on an already-stretched global fuel market and further raising prices globally.

items: If Trump bans U.S. diesel exports, global prices will go even higher, experts say

blocks.text: A new AP-NORC poll found that a majority of U.S. adults blame Trump for higher prices, and approval on his handling of the economy hit a new low.

articles.title: Iran accused of blocking SIM cards, digital access to silence dissent
articles.summary: DW has spoken with several Iranians who say their SIM cards, bank access and online accounts were blocked until they deleted critical content or pledged to stop activism.

image.caption: Social media users in Iran say their SIM cards were blocked after posting political content or liking posts on InstagramImage: UGC/AFP

blocks.text: In Iran, cell phone numbers are a key tool for digital identity verification and access to banking, judicial, administrative and insurance services, as well as many everyday activities.
As a result, disconnecting a SIM card can do more than block calls and text messages. It can also cut off access to a wide range of digital services.

Some Iranians said the restrictions on their cell phones were accompanied by the blocking of user accounts and access to banking and government services. They said access was restored only after they deleted critical content or pledged to stop participating in protest-related activities.
DW spoke to three people in Iran about the issue. They have used pseudonyms out of concern for their safety.
'Six hours of interrogation'
Sina told DW that he realized his SIM card had been disconnected while returning from university and trying to book a taxi by phone.

The 25-year-old said that after visiting a telecommunications center, he received a call from someone claiming to be from the Intelligence Organization of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IO-IRGC), who instructed him to go to a specified location to have his SIM card reconnected.

blocks.caption: A message on Instagram stating: 'The activities of the page are in accodance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran' Image: unbekannt

blocks.text: Sina said he was interrogated for about six hours and that his mobile phone was confiscated.

He said the return of his SIM card and phone was made conditional on signing a pledge expressing "remorse" for his activist activities and online "propaganda against the system." He said he was also required to publish posts supporting the Islamic Republic to "prove his brotherhood with the system."

Several hours later, he said, his family discovered that posts on his Instagram account had been deleted. Only one remained, stating that "the activities of the page are in accordance with the laws of the Islamic Republic of Iran."
A month later, he said, he had still not received his SIM card or mobile phone back and was unable to access his social media accounts.

Sorour, a 41-year-old translator at an official translation office in Tehran, said that after her SIM card was disconnected, she went to a location designated by the IO-IRGC, where she was interrogated for hours about her activities on Instagram and X.
Revolutionary Guard has 'massive' role in clampdown: expert

Sorour said she was told to make her account private and pledge to refrain from activities critical of the authorities, including advocating for political prisoners, protesting executions and supporting demonstrators during nationwide anti-government protests that began in late December 2025.

Mina, who lives in Isfahan, said she was summoned by an institution she identified as the IRGC Intelligence Organization after posting a comment supporting one of the country's political currents under a post by a foreign-based news outlet.
The 63-year-old said her SIM card and national identification card were blocked after she refused to comply with the summons.
According to Mina, the restrictions disrupted her access to bank transfers, administrative systems, online purchases and services that require electronic identity verification and one-time passwords.
She told DW she had also been denied access to Sana, the judiciary's electronic system, and was therefore unable to determine whether a case or charges had been filed against her.
SIM cards: the key to digital life in Iran
Several other Iranian citizens also posted similar complaints on social media.
Zia Nabavi, a former political prisoner, said in an Instagram post that his SIM card had been suddenly disconnected.
He said he discovered the issue while at a doctor's office, where he needed access to his mobile phone and banking text messages.

"For a long time, I have come to the conclusion that the government's policy toward critics and opponents is to apply pressure that pushes them toward obedience or withdrawing from their activities," Nabavi wrote.
Regime 'taking the Iranian people hostage'
Reyhaneh Saeedi, a physician and activist, also said on Instagram that her SIM card has been blocked for months and that this is the second time she has faced such restrictions.
She said the measure has effectively prevented her from practicing medicine, issuing prescriptions and renewing her Medical Council and medical office licenses.

Saeedi said her identification card had also been deactivated. She added that no ruling had been formally served on her, she had not been informed of any charges or judicial proceedings, and her efforts to determine the reason for the restrictions had yielded no results.
Actress Shaghayegh Dehghan said on Instagram that her SIM card had been blocked and that she did not know which institution or authority was behind the move.
Cutting communications

The disconnection of SIM cards and other digital restrictions has become part of a broader set of tools that the Islamic Republic has used over the past four decades to exert pressure on opponents, critics, journalists, and civil and human rights activists.
The Defending Free Flow of Information (DeFFI) organization reported in 2025 that journalists and activists had their SIM cards blocked without judicial orders.
The measures have raised concerns about the powers exercised by security institutions to deny citizens access to communication tools and essential services.
They have also highlighted the absence of a clear accountability mechanism, leaving those affected with no obvious avenue to challenge the restrictions or seek an explanation.

articles.title: COA flags DepEd contract delays impacting textbooks, learning materials delivery
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged delays in the Department of Education"s (DepEd) signing of contracts with suppliers of textbooks and other learning materials, which affected their timely…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 11:17pm

The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged delays in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) signing of contracts with suppliers of textbooks and other learning materials, which affected their timely distribution to schools.

According to a "24 Oras" report by Mariz Umali, COA said the signing of 56 contracts worth nearly P2.5 billion for textbooks and teachers’ manuals for Grades 2, 5, and 8 was delayed by up to nearly 60 days.
This was well beyond the 10-calendar-day period prescribed under procurement rules following the issuance of the Notice of Award (NOA).

The delays also affected other learning resources, including self-learning modules, the inspection and acceptance of supplemental learning resources, and some project implementation activities, COA said.
The timely delivery of these materials is particularly important as schools increasingly resort to online and asynchronous classes during periods of inclement weather.
Textbooks and other instructional materials also allow students to continue studying at home even without a teacher physically present.
In its response to COA, DepEd explained that the process was not simple, as 56 separate contracts had to be processed, each requiring independent preparation, legal review and possible revisions.
COA, however, said these processes were mandatory and that DepEd’s Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) should have monitored compliance with the prescribed timeline for contract signing.
COA said DepEd had agreed to review its processes to ensure compliance with procurement rules and prevent similar delays.
GMA News is still awaiting DepEd’s response to the audit findings. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: US Coast Guard says it has intercepted ship carrying fuel to Cuba
articles.summary:
US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues

The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship…

blocks.text: The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound for Cuba, as the ⁠Trump administration’s crippling ⁠oil embargo against ​the island nation continued.

The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in the Caribbean Sea between Cuba ⁠and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship ⁠was 91 metres (300ft) long.
“Grace was transiting to Cuba, carrying fuel, ​and was believed to be employing ‌tactics common amongst the ‌dark fleet,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.

A Coast Guard team ‌boarded the ship and escorted it to Mexico, where a Mexican navy inspection team “confirmed the presence of large quantities of fuel in the vessel’s ballast tanks”. The vessel was also carrying several containers believed to contain illicit fuel, the statement said.

The Trump administration has openly stated ‌that its goal is to change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put the country ​under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

Oil shipments from Cuba’s traditional suppliers, Venezuela and Mexico, ended abruptly after the US ousted the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. US Coast Guard ⁠cutters patrol the waters off Cuba, while sanctions and threats have dissuaded ​tankers from even ​setting sail.

“The high seas ​are not a sanctuary for lawlessness,” Adm Kevin Lunday, the commandant ​of the Coast ‌Guard, said. “Dark fleet ​actors who employ ​deceptive tactics to engage in illicit activities will not evade justice.”
The statement did not say how authorities knew the fuel was headed to Cuba or how much fuel Grace was carrying.

articles.title: Woman in fake nurse case once again avoids sentencing after 6th postponement
articles.summary: Lisa Driscoll didn't show up to court on Thursday for what was supposed to be her long-awaited sentencing hearing. Lucky for her, the judge wasn't there either.

image.caption: Lisa Driscoll is shown in court in Gander, N.L., in a file photo. (Troy Turner/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Lisa Driscoll didn't show up to court on Thursday for what was supposed to be her long-awaited sentencing hearing. Lucky for her, the judge wasn't there either.
Lisa Driscoll catches a break as judge is absent from court on Thursday
Lisa Driscoll, a woman who stole other people’s nursing credentials to gain employment in Newfoundland on multiple occasions, has once again avoided sentencing.

She was a no-show in provincial court on Thursday in St. John’s after being ordered by Judge Bruce Short at her last appearance to be there in person. In a twist of fate for the convicted fake nurse, the judge was also absent from the courtroom on Thursday.

Judge Paul Noble presided over the appearance on Short’s behalf. Driscoll’s new lawyer, Philip Warren, was asking for an adjournment regardless, saying Driscoll claimed to be sick and was either in the hospital, or on the way to the hospital.
“This is the sixth request for a postponement,” Crown prosecutor Deidre Badcock said before pulling out her notebook to quote Short from the last appearance in July.

“He said, ‘You be here unless it is life or death,’” Badcock read. “‘The court has given you great leeway and ample opportunity to comply and you continue to not. You will not get any further appointments or adjournments. You will be sentenced on Oct. 1.’”
But that wasn’t the case.
Badcock then asked the judge for an arrest warrant, saying the only way Driscoll will be present for her sentencing is if she is held in custody until her next court date.
“I just find it really harsh, I really do,” Warren said.

items: Woman with history of impersonating nurses cleared of theft charge
Woman impersonated registered nurse at Gander long-term care home, says health authority

blocks.text: Noble decided against issuing a warrant for Driscoll’s arrest, instead making an order that she be present in person for her next appearance.
Badcock said it’s become routine for Driscoll to seek delays, without providing any evidence to support her applications for adjournment.

“I trust what [Warren] says his client has told him, but I don’t trust anything his client tells him because we’ve consistently been told she’s in the hospital, or she’s having surgery or she’s having X or having Y. And she has not been able to produce a single piece of paper, not even a printout from her actual online health-care app, which we all have.”
The case will be called again on Oct. 7 at 9 a.m. to find a new date for sentencing.
Driscoll first pleaded guilty to her charges on May 12, 2025.
She's fired two lawyers in 2026, which also led to significant delays.
Driscoll used fake names, licences to get jobs
Lisa Driscoll, who also went by the name Lisa Strickland at times, was convicted of criminal negligence causing death in relation to the 2017 death of her four-year-old son in Ontario.
That conviction and subsequent prison sentence left her unable to pass a code of conduct check in Ontario.

Driscoll came back to Newfoundland, where she hails from, and used the legitimate licence number of a licensed practical nurse with a similar name to get a job at Chancellor Park, a nursing home in St. John’s, in March of 2021.
While working there, Driscoll used the same stolen licence to get a second job at Kenny’s Pond retirement home in St. John’s.

Alarm bells were raised when Driscoll applied for another job with Lane’s Retirement Homes in July of 2022. The College of Licensed Practical Nurses got a call from a representative of the company, looking to check her licensing information. They found none of her information matched the information of the person who held the legitimate licence in the system.

Police began investigating, and reached out to the province’s health authority, which confirmed it also had a job application on file from Driscoll in which she used the licence number of another nurse with a similar name.
After being fired from her positions in St. John’s and while the investigation was still ongoing, Driscoll was discovered to be working at a retirement home in Gander — this time as a travel nurse.
Driscoll was accused of stealing medication from that home in Gander, but was acquitted in March of 2026.
