articles.title: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.summary: The former employees were investigated for sharing data with an outside AI evaluation group.

blocks.text: OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.
The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.
The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.
Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.
OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.
In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.
That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.
Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

articles.title: Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case
articles.summary: The BBC's Nada Tawfik was at the hearing, where the university's Student Assembly led a discussion around safety concerns and sexual violence on campus.

blocks.text: Anger and concern about student safety and rape culture on campus was discussed at a public hearing led by the Student Assembly of Cornell University.

The hearing was held in response to an investigation into the alleged rape of a woman at Cornell University in 2024. The woman, being referred to as Jane Doe, has filed a civil lawsuit against the university alleging she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house on campus.
Cornell has rejected claims that it failed to punish those involved. It has also agreed to have the case examined by an independent investigator.
The BBC's Nada Tawfik spoke to students who attended the public hearing.

articles.title: EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
articles.summary: The proposals include setting up so-called return hubs outside the EU and strengthening the border agency Frontex. Greece has even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency…

image.caption: The EU wants to implement tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns [FILE: April 5, 2019]Image: picture-alliance/NurPhoto/N. Economou

blocks.text: The interior ministers of European Union countries met in Luxembourg on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen border controls and curb undocumented migration into the 27-member bloc.
Following the talks, they approved a new regulation to boost deportations of irregular migrants.
It will allow member states ​to establish so-called return hubs outside the EU for migrants who are legally required to leave the bloc but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
Countries including Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy and set up such migrant centers.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance
What did the ministers say?
"When it comes to return hubs," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters, "it's progressing very well."
"We are moving in the right direction," he said without providing further details.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said there were "preliminary" talks on return hubs but declined to say which countries were involved.
More work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits, he said.
"These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term," Dobrindt noted, adding that he was nevertheless hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said a technical mission already visited a potential host country in early September.
Supporters of the policy say return hubs could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
But critics question their legality and argue that they violate migrants' fundamental rights.
Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing
Suspending asylum process in emergencies?
On Thursday, Greece even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations. The right to seek asylum is guaranteed by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
Athens argued that current rules are inadequate to handle mass arrivals as in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.

The Spanish government estimates over 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most of them have since returned, some 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some EU capitals for a tougher approach. The Spanish government has said only minors and small groups of the people who entered Ceuta were brought to mainland Spain.
Greece's proposal appeared to draw support from some member states.

"We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure," said Dutch Migration Minister van den Brink. "In situations like Ceuta, it should be treated as ​a border management issue rather than an asylum issue."

Asked whether he saw a suspension of asylum as possible under the new emergency law, ​Magnus Brunner, EU commissioner for migration, said: "Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times," while stressing that "we will always comply with fundamental rights and values."
How the EU compromised its values on migration
Plans to curtail irregular migration
The interior ministers' talks come as undocumented migration remains high on the EU's political agenda, with far-right parties increasingly gaining support across the bloc.
The situation has pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this month that the Commission will propose an emergency tool for countries to better deal with mass migration movements.
But details are still being worked out.
There are also plans to strengthen the EU's border agency, Frontex, with many stressing the need for the organization to have a rapid intervention force that could intervene in border crises.

articles.title: Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
articles.summary: A voter mobilisation campaign has registered huge numbers of young people but it is not clear who they are backing.

blocks.text: Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.

The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.

"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."

Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.

"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.

More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.

He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.

"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.

He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.

I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.

"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.

"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."

"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.

"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.

"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."

He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."

Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.

The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.

"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."

Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

articles.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
articles.summary: Amid global tumult, the two countries alliance is not the only unlikely pairing.

blocks.text: Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.

Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.

"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.

"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."

Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."

According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.

"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.
But there's also the question of security.

On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.

"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.

No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.

"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.
In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".

Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.

In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.

In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.

There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".
He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.
With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.
But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.

He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.

That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.

Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.

However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.
Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.
Top image credit: PA / Nur Photo via Getty images

articles.title: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.summary: Several self-inflicted mistakes have cost the biggest sportswear brand on the planet in recent years.

blocks.text: It's been a difficult few years for Nike.
The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.
The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.

Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint.
However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.
The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.

To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years.
Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.
So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?

Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available.
"The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.
Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products.
"They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."
The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today.
The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.
In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.
While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024.

"[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."
Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.
However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.
Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".
Was that a parting dig at Nike?
For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance.
"Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says.
"When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.
Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.
Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn (£8.3bn), which undershot analysts' expectations.
Notably, the company cited "headwinds" in China, where revenue declined by 26%.

articles.title: The wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fall
articles.summary: Cuban exiles in Florida are increasingly hopeful that regime change in Cuba is now on the horizon.

blocks.text: This influential community of Cuban exiles has detested the Communist-run government ever since the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro expropriated their lands and nationalised their families' companies after taking power in 1959.
And they have wielded their political and economic clout in Florida over the years to shape Washington's policies towards their homeland.
Sixto fled the island as a teenager. Now a real estate developer in his early 80s, his organisation is drafting plans for what he calls "the day after" in Cuba.
The CANCC has created a proposal for a Cuban Stock Exchange and formed committees on everything from energy infrastructure to food security.
Post-Communist planning is nothing new in Miami.
Countless documents and logistical plans have been drawn up by interest groups over the decades, some of them more sober and measured than others.

The difference now, insists Sixto, is the Trump administration's push to force total change on the island. And he says they have the ear of some high-profile contacts including people close to the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio.
"Together with deliveries of humanitarian aid and medical supplies, we'd go and do business in Cuba right away," says Sixto.
In Cuba itself, such claims are mostly met with scepticism.

In the face of Washington's "maximum pressure" campaign on Cuba, the island's leadership recently announced 176 economic liberalisation measures. The Cuban President, Miguel Díaz-Canel, said they were "to advance the defence of socialism, to support and widen social justice".

To his critics, they look distinctly like full-blown capitalism - lifting the cap on the number of workers in a private business, allowing the direct hiring and firing of Cuban employees and permitting ownership of multiple enterprises at once, including by Cuban Americans.

Still, the attendees at the CANCC meeting dismissed the economic reforms as cosmetic, saying they gave no meaningful guarantees to investors. They would "not put a foot into Cuba", Sixto said, while the current regime remained in place.

Some analysts think such planning meetings are premature. Although Cuban Americans are convinced that change is imminent in Cuba, none can say with any certainty what it will be - a US military operation as seen in Venezuela in January? Or a new economic pact with the island's leadership?

"Right now, the very high expectations created by the US administration that some kind of 'day after' was coming soon, or that Cuba would 'be next' have been kicked down the road," says Mike Bustamante, associate professor of history at the University of Miami.

With the November mid-term elections in the US approaching and the Trump administration embroiled in the "quagmire" of the Iran war, Bustamante argues there is little appetite for further foreign adventures.
"It's really tough to think that they will escalate further than what they're doing which is this drip-drip-drip of sanctions."

With the island's oil supply effectively shut off since January, that is already a significant escalation, says Mike Bustamente. Although they have made life unbearable for most ordinary people, they haven't yet "created the ingredients for a political inflection point" in Cuba, he adds.
The Cuban government has not commented on the CANCC itself. But traditionally such groups prompt indignation among revolutionaries who insist they will not be forced out by their critics in Miami.

I ask some guests if they can appreciate the irony that the same people who support a major source of the island's misery – the decades-long US economic embargo and the current fuel blockade – are now hatching plans for its reconstruction, without the input of most Cubans.

For Cuban-American agricultural expert Hugo Orizondo it is only practical to draw up a road map to Cuban development. "Right now, Cuba is like a black hole, we don't know what is happening over there," he admits. "But we do know the potential [for investment]."

Orizondo says he understands the reticence among Cubans to see foreign investors buying up something as sensitive as the rights to arable land. "But what are they going to do with it?" he retorts. "When investors come, they bring money and technology into the land."
Both are urgently needed, he says, if Cuba is ever to produce enough to feed its own population and break its reliance on food imports.

Land titles lie at the heart of any reconstruction project put forward by this generation of wealthy Cuban Americans. Juan Omar Sixto says his father lost five properties and a farm in Cuba's Pinar del Rio province to the revolution. While he insists he has no intention of removing any family living in those homes, he does want compensation for the nationalised land.
"I worked on that farm for five years of my life with my father, and they took it away. I want restitution or compensation. Even if they give me just a penny on the dollar, I'll take it."
"It's moral justice," he argues.

The Cuban government portrays such historic title claims as bitterness by a corrupt landed gentry who made fortunes on the backs of indentured workers and slaves. Both slavery and the system of indentured workers didn't end in Cuba until the late 19th Century.
The government also argues that the exiles could never stand that Castro passed land reforms which handed over their fields to the workers and the state.

"Most of our sugar mills have been dismantled, but we will recover those lands and put them into production," says Nicolás Gutiérrez, the president of the National Association of Sugar Mill Owners of Cuba, an exile organisation championing the title claims.
"I'm not promising it will be in sugar," he says.

"It might be in ethanol, co-generation, solar panels or water purification cells. Who knows? There are a lot of different options," he remarks. "We need to get them producing, we need to have a real wage paid to Cuban workers and create a multiplier economic effect across the island."

With the ice clinking in their drinks and a cool breeze rustling the palm trees on the perfectly manicured lawn, the CANCC members make it sound easy. But within hours of their gathering, Cuba had descended into its sixth nationwide blackout this year.
The disconnection between the hopes for change in Miami and the realities on the ground in Cuba is stark. Many Miami-based Cubans think the monumental shift they have prayed for is almost here.

If so, it will inevitably bring huge social and humanitarian disruption which the stricken island is ill-equipped to cope with. Even assuming the diaspora's support is well-intentioned rather than purely self-interested, fixing the island's failing electrical grid alone is estimated to cost $8bn to $10bn (£6bn to £7.5bn).

Before any industry in Cuba – from agriculture to tourism – can be revitalised by the exiles' wealth and political connections, Cubans continue to face acute shortages in food, water, fuel and medicines. Miami's ambitious plans aside, most Cubans just hope their days get a little easier sometime soon.

articles.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
articles.summary: It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp has won his first game as Germany boss, after replacing Julian Nagelsmann after the World CupImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.
"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.
Bischof gets first goal on home turf

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

blocks.caption: Florian Wirtz (left) and Tom Bischof were Germay's goalscorersImage: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/AFP

blocks.text: "It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.
"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."
Klopp: 'I liked everything'
While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.
It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."
Wirtz provides spark and hope

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

articles.title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
articles.summary:
Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’, as nation prepares to go to polls

Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro, Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington

blocks.text: Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.

Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.

Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.
According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.

Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

In recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused of meddling in Brazilian affairs by using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.

Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”

Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.”

The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that the Trump administration was pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.
A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.
Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.

Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping his constitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.
During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.
Bolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.

Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.

The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.”

Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.

articles.title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin insists Moscow is "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders.

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers it has come under direct attack in its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.

Addressing the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin insisted Russia was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that Moscow was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.

Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing it is a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.

Last week alone Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
In a wide-ranging speech, the Russian leader told his audience he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.

Although Putin himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that it had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries, and on its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war on Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, and a key bridge in Kyiv was attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.

"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.

He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea which he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.

"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".

Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly fire at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten, and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

articles.title: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, CBC's Johanna Wagstaffe shares the vibe at New York Climate Week, and what she learned from meteorologists there; we map out Canada's progress on…

image.caption: Grabbing a quick moment outside the WNYC radio studio before heading in to record. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hi, it's Johanna. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the weather we experience every day. But after spending Climate Week in New York with fellow meteorologists from across North America, one thing is clear: this job is getting deeply personal.
This week:

items: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals
Mycelium with your meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

blocks.text: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

I was invited to join a closed-door workshop in New York City during Climate Week called "Beyond the Forecast: How Trusted Weather Voices Can Help Communities Understand Climate and Extreme Weather." Hosted by the Clinton Global Initiative in partnership with the Eleven Eleven Foundation, the session offered a rare space to talk openly with other broadcast meteorologists about how we communicate climate change.

I mean, this is my bread and butter. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the everyday weather we experience. I've been grateful to have the support, platforms and formats at CBC to do just that.

Even so, there is a distinct weight to this work — seeing the data play out in real time, knowing the severity of a storm's impact before it hits, and navigating how politicized the term "climate change" has become. Stepping into my new role as the host of CBC's climate podcast What on Earth?, the timing couldn't have been better for this gathering.
Finding common ground in New York

Arriving in New York, I loved being recognized by fellow Canadians at Newark Airport — climate advisers from Vancouver headed to the same gathering. It was a nice reminder of why these conferences matter. Bringing people together (despite the carbon footprint of travel) creates a momentum you can't replicate virtually.

Walking from the subway up 5th Avenue toward the conference centre on my first day, I instinctively fell into the fast-paced ebb and flow of the city street. I credit my former Toronto days for my defensive walking skills, but adopting that rhythm makes you feel immediately plugged in. This trip was going to be all about feeling part of something bigger.

The workshop itself was one I won't soon forget. Nearly every major meteorologist I've watched on U.S. networks was there (plus Bill Nye!). Our scheduled two-hour session ran long — after all, we talk for a living — but it was deeply cathartic. Hearing forecasters from Fox News to CNN to ABC, alongside scientists and policy-makers, open up about the shared challenges of communicating climate risk felt like a rare moment of unity.
Here are a few takeaways I can share:
1. The connection between weather and climate is undeniable — but the pushback is real
Underlying every discussion in that room was one overarching reality: we are all trying to talk about climate change as station scientists.

The science behind extreme weather is indisputable. But for television forecasters attempting to bring that science into daily broadcasts, the pushback from audiences can be tough — and deeply emotional. While I've been lucky enough to avoid the absolute worst of it, let's just say you never truly develop a thick skin. And knowing what lies ahead when forecasting a devastating storm carries a real weight.

Between sessions, I raced from Midtown down to SOHO to record in the studios at WNYC (New York public radio) — a fun moment of solidarity, hopping from one public broadcaster's home base to another. But the conversation I recorded hit home sharply. I spoke with forecaster Chris Gloninger, who made the difficult decision to leave his TV news career after facing severe harassment and a death threat simply for explaining climate links on air.

But Chris's story was a stark reminder that serving as a trusted voice often comes at a high personal cost. To go "beyond the forecast," weather communicators need more than just thick skin — we need strong community support to keep having these vital conversations safely.
2. U.S. and Canadian TV live in different broadcast universes

I attended the workshop alongside only one other Canadian: my friend Mark Robinson from The Weather Network, who I went to meteorology school with! Being there together highlighted how much the U.S. and Canada have in common, and also just how differently our two media markets operate.

American broadcast TV remains deeply traditional, with millions of viewers still tuning in to local 6 o'clock newscasts every night. For U.S. forecasters, that means trying to cram complex climate attribution science into a lightning-fast, two-minute weather window between commercial breaks.

At CBC, as the media landscape has shifted, we've chosen to experiment with meeting audiences where they are. Beyond dedicated space on podcasts like What On Earth? and digital platforms, our local TV markets frequently carve out extra airtime specifically to connect the dots between severe weather and climate change. Having that room to explain why a heat wave or atmospheric river is happening is something I was reminded not to take for granted — because in a tight TV hit, context is often the first thing left on the cutting-room floor. But as more U.S. newsrooms experiment with climate-dedicated segments and digital extras, the potential to inform communities is huge. It shows that when we give trusted weather voices room to breathe, audiences gain a far better understanding of the world shifting around them.

Stepping out of those closed-door rooms in New York, I was reminded that connecting those dots on air isn't always easy, and it certainly isn't always comfortable — but as extreme weather becomes our daily reality, it's a conversation we're more committed than ever to having.
— Johanna Wagstaffe
Old issues of What on Earth? are here. The CBC News climate page is here.

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode: When a meteorologist took a job in Iowa, he was excited to make his forecasts matter to viewers by bringing in climate impacts that were relevant to their lives, like rising costs and energy independence. But then the backlash began, escalating to a death threat.

He's not the only one. At climate week in New York City, a group of meteorologists gathered to share stories about speaking to often polarized audiences. When facts become political, how can climate change's frontline communicators stick to the science?

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen. The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.
Reader feedback
Last week, we told you about a unique air quality meets wearable art project that's trying to bring awareness about dangerous pollutants especially when we can't see them.

Edwina Hylton wrote in with an important point: "In the eventuality that the device shows serious pollution, what is the person wearing the device supposed to do? Fine to know things are bad, but if there isn't a reasonable alternative, what is the point in collecting the information?"
While not always equitable or within reach, some experts we've spoken to over the years have said awareness gives a power of choice to take action, like wearing a mask or moving indoors.
And, for some, like reader Maureen Moffat, awareness is a click away. She writes, "I check the air quality daily on the net. Easy."
Got questions, comments, or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)
The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Four years ago, Canada welcomed negotiators from around the world to strike a historic deal on protecting nature. The conference was supposed to be in China, but it was 2022 and the COVID-weary government there had decided not to host.

So the meeting reverted to Montreal, which hosts the secretariat of the UN treaty that governs biological diversity, and I jumped on a train to go cover it. Canada led negotiations to land a new global target: protecting 30 per cent of lands and oceans by 2030. And it decided to lead by example by embarking on its own ambitious conservation agenda.
Here's a map of Canada's protected spaces. Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans so far.

And a new assessment says there's progress internationally — the world will reach 27 per cent protection on land by 2030. For oceans, protection will only reach 12 per cent. I spoke to Steven Guilbeault, Canada's former environment minister and the guy who helped land that deal in Montreal, about why we are falling short — and also why he's still optimistic countries will ramp up the fight against biodiversity loss.
— Inayat Singh
Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

items: A man in Squamish, B.C., has put his Halloween zombie decoration out early — to keep bears out of his garbage bins. See how the bears are responding in this CBC News video.

Kids are being toilet trained later and later. That's costing parents in money spent on diapers and time spent on additional gross diaper changes. But it's also creating a lot more plastic waste. A new study calculates the environmental cost, and offers some solutions.

Mountainous, densely populated Japan doesn't have many places to put large solar farms, but it has found a solution in a type of infrastructure that proliferated in the economic boom of the 1980s and is now disused.
A new study shows electric trucks are becoming cheaper to operate than their diesel counterparts and how quickly the savings can outstrip the higher up-front cost in some European countries.

Canada's Building Canada Strong Act is supposed to speed up infrastructure projects. But it could also dismantle environmental safeguards that protect Canadians and prevent wildlife from extinction, despite the federal government claiming otherwise, environmental groups tell CBC's David Thurton and Olivia Stefanovich.

blocks.text: Mycelium meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs
If fermented liquid fungus from a bioreactor doesn't sound like your idea of a delicious meal, the folks at Maia Farms say, don't knock it 'til you've tried it.
The Vancouver-based company has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms.
"The bioreactor allows us to control the environment in which the mycelium are grown," said chief innovation officer Sean Lacoursiere.
"It allows us to keep everything moving and grooving and it also allows us to aerate and provide all the oxygen that the mushroom will need."
Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants
The result is a food product that can be mixed with different protein sources to add bulk and enhance a meal's nutritional profile.
While mushroom products are often used in meat substitutes, one of Maia's target markets is the meat industry itself.
"We can add a lot of nutritional, taste and texture benefits while reducing the amount of meat that's required," Lacoursiere said.
The offering couldn't be timelier for restaurateurs and other food retailers struggling to keep costs down as the price of meat soars.
According to Canada Beef, retail beef averaged $28 per kilogram in April, up 15 per cent from a year ago and close to a record high.
Maia Farms' director of food science and innovation Karen McAfee said mycelium could replace between 25 and 40 per cent of the meat in items like sausage rolls, meatballs and burger patties.
"It can help retain moisture… it can also help with the high level of umami flavour," she said.
Better for the planet
The benefits of hiding mushrooms in your meat go beyond the financial.
"From our estimates, we produce around two kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of material," Lacoursiere said.
According to a 2024 report by the Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef, one kilogram of consumed boneless beef in Canada produces 32.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide.
The same amount also requires 1,912 litres of water, almost four times the 500 litres Maia reports in its process.
"I don't think people really comprehend just how much of a difference this type of product can make," he said.
Finding consumers
While meat alternatives are readily available in Canadian supermarkets, sales in the sector have been declining for several years.
Lacoursiere is hoping Maia has what it takes to buck the trend.
"The whole goal of our company here is to produce mycelium at large scales, at a very cost competitive level. And we're already seeing that," he said.
As for the "ick" factor?
"It's an oyster mushroom. It's been eaten for hundreds, if not thousands of years. It's delicious. We just found a way to grow it in a submerged liquid state."
— Ruby Cornish

articles.title: Latvians head to the polls with Russia on their minds
articles.summary: On October 3, Latvians will elect a new parliament with Russia looming large over the campaign. Security fears dominate the agenda, but so does a debate over the economic cost of cutting ties with…

image.caption: Latvia goes to the polls for parliamentary elections on October 3, 2026.Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3.
Security fears ahead of elections

Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded.

In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet.

On top of that there are hybrid threats, including migrant flows that Latvia and its neighbors say are being encouraged by Russia's ally Belarus to pressure the EU and test border security. Intelligence officials of several European countries, including Latvia and the Czech Republic have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO in the upcoming "months, not years."

blocks.caption: Guard on the Latvian-Russian border.Image: Gints Ivuskans/AFP

blocks.text: "There are concerns in the West and also here in the Baltic states that Russia might be trying some further actions here in the Baltics," says Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. "If you want to test NATO, there is no better place than the Baltic states."
Near-unanimous agreement on defense

Latvia elects its 100-seat parliament, Saeima, through proportional representation, meaning coalition governments are the norm. Polls currently put the centrist United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ahead, followed by the populist alliance Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and Latvia First led by Ainars Slesers. The center-left Progressives and the conservative National Alliance are also expected to enter parliament.
Most of these Latvian parties view Russia as a security challenge.

"The biggest threat is our neighbors, Russia and Belarus," says Agnese Kupca of the United List. "Our partners in the EU should understand: it is not only our border with Russia, but also EU and NATO border with aggressor."

Latvia is one of the few NATO members that have committed by law to spending 5% of GDP on defense, and analysts say the country's foreign policy orientation is unlikely to change regardless of which coalition emerges after the vote as there is nearly unanimous consensus on the importance of NATO. Which is backed by their voters: according to Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Security Radar 2025 Latvians generally have a positive view of NATO.

blocks.caption: Unites List election campaign poster featuring Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs before the general election in Riga, Latvia.Image: Ints Kalnins/REUTERS

blocks.text: Economic concerns among voters
But while security policy enjoys broad agreement, the economic consequences of Latvia distancing itself from Russia remain contentious.

Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was among Latvia's most important trading partners. Since 2022, Latvia has reduced imports from Russia and Belarus by more than 90% and introduced some of the toughest restrictions in the EU on goods from the two countries. Latvia's economy has adapted, but businesses with strong pre-war links to Russia were among the hardest hit.

"This closeness to the theater of war has strongly influenced the investment climate," says political analyst Filips Rajevskis. "So the big question is how to increase the investments and grow the economy."

Many Latvians reject any economic cooperation with Russia on security grounds. Sixty percent said they want Latvia to reduce dependence on Russia, according to FES Security Radar 2025. "In the current situation, it's absolute nonsense. We can't watch what's happening and still be friends with Russia," one passerby in Riga told DW.
Not breaking up with Russia completely?
At the same time 20% of Latvians, according to FES, favor closer ties with Russia. Calls for a more pragmatic approach towards its eastern neighbor are not uncommon in the political debates.
Julija Stepanenko, leader of Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, has repeatedly argued against completely severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus.

Earlier this year, it emerged that Stepanenko has received gifts worth roughly €400,000 ($470,000) from her father, a Russia-based businessman whose company manufactures construction materials, including anti-tank fortifications known as "dragon's teeth." But despite that, her party remains in second place in the polls.

When DW met Lyubov Shvetsova, one of Sovereign Power/Union of New Latvians party candidates at a campaign stand just outside the center of Riga, she rejected accusations that the party is pro-Russian.
"Our approach is pragmatism oriented toward the interests of Latvian business," she said.
Economic pragmatism
Another advocate of a more pragmatic economic approach is Ainars Slesers, former businessman and leader of Latvia First.
During an interview on Latvian public television earlier in September, Slesers argued that transit of goods with Russia should continue as long as it is not prohibited by EU sanctions.

His party has focused heavily on economic issues, arguing that Latvia should prioritize growth and investment over what it sees as excessive self-imposed restrictions. And this approach has found support: more than 9% are ready to vote for Latvia First, which is in third place in the polls.
However, discussions about fully restoring trade with Russia are premature, party member Edmunds Zivtins told DW. "As long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing, we cannot talk about it," he said.
Language and identity dividing Latvia
Analysts say such parties may attract some voters who feel alienated by Latvia's increasingly restrictive approach toward Russia.

blocks.caption: Golden roofs atop Saints Boris and Gleb Orthodox Cathedral are seen over trees in the centre of Daugavpils, eastern Latvia.Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: The appeal is not necessarily driven by support for the Kremlin. Rather, it often comes from parts of the country's Russian-speaking minority who feel overlooked by mainstream parties and uneasy about policies such as the phase-out of Russian-language school education and the reduced role of Russian in public life.
About one-third of Latvia's population speaks Russian at home.
However, the outcome of these elections is hard to predict. Filips Rajevskis says many voters are hiding not only their party preference, but even their decision to go to vote ahead of elections.

As Latvians head to the polls, Moscow is shaping the campaign in ways both direct and indirect: as a security threat driving support for NATO and defense spending, and as an economic and cultural question that continues to divide parts of the electorate.

articles.title: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza
articles.summary:
Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems

The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s…

blocks.text: The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.

In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.

At the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.
While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets in Gaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.

The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanied death threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.

It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.

“The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.

Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.
A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZA as junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.
“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.

blocks.caption: People walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings in Jabaliya in the northern Gaza Strip. Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters

blocks.text: “The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.

“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.

“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”

While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.

articles.title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
articles.summary: Lawyers for Good's family say US officials created "an unprecedented environment for state sponsored violence" in Minneapolis.

blocks.text: The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.
Renee Good was killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a sweep of the city targeting immigrants and criminals that was called Operation Metro Surge.

One of the suits blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family, Antonio Romanucci, said during a news conference on Thursday.
The White House and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) have not yet commented on the lawsuits.
After another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the Minnesota city.
The lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and her brother Brent Ganger.
